title: Family rejects ICE accusations Iowa City mom used fake ID | News | thegazette.com
authors: Vanessa Miller, Vanessa Miller The Gazette, Vanessa MillerThe Gazette
description: The family of an Iowa City mother facing deportation after being detained by ICE on her way to work last week is denying the federal agency’s accusations that she used a fake birth certificate and passport to enter the United States.
text:
Fatou Traore (center) and her family pose in Iowa City.

IOWA CITY — The family of an Iowa City mother facing deportation after being detained by ICE on her way to work last week is denying the federal agency’s accusations that she used a fake birth certificate and passport to enter the United States.

“That’s false information,” Esoumaila Diallo, 19, said on behalf of his mother, Fatou Traore, 43, who is being held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at its Richwood Correctional Center in Monroe, Louisiana.

Diallo is responding to a statement ICE issued Thursday following calls across the community and state that it return Traore to her family in Iowa City — where she left behind a husband and four sons, ages 3 to 19.

“Traore has a final removal order from 2011 and admitted to using a fake birth certificate and fake passport to enter the U.S. at an unknown time and location,” an ICE media contact told The Gazette after confirming its officers arrested Traore — calling her “an illegal alien from the Ivory Coast” — during a “targeted enforcement operation Sept. 24 in Iowa City, Iowa.”

“ICE is applying the law as written. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.”

Diallo said he doesn’t know where ICE got its information and hasn’t heard about any removal order or judge ruling his mother should be deported. She has no criminal history.

“Talked to mom, and she also said she’s never said that,” he told The Gazette after speaking with his mother by phone. “Every time they asked her to sign things or questions she requested her lawyer.”

Attorneys advocating for Traore provided The Gazette with a 2011 “withholding of removal” order — preventing her deportation back to the Ivory Coast, where she immigrated from due to safety concerns. They also provided The Gazette with a photo of Traore’s most recent U.S. employment authorization card — good through March 2029.

And she’s listed online as a UI employee — working as a custodian alongside her husband Oumar Diallo, 56, and her sister Haby Diallo, 32, who witnessed Traore’s detention last week by unidentified men in unmarked vehicles.

Traore was quickly transported to the holding facility in Louisiana, where she’s been told she’s being deported to Sierra Leone — a place she’s never been.

In its statement to The Gazette, ICE said, “Third-country agreements, which ensure due process under the U.S. Constitution, are essential to the safety of our homeland and the American people.”

“We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Home App,” according to the statement. “The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

Traore’s arrest came a day after the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Sept. 23 blocked third-country deportations — calling them unlawful in that they deprive immigrants of the opportunity to object or raise safety concerns. Under that order, Traore’s deportation would have been illegal. And, in fact, it forced the cancellation of at least one flight carrying 70 people to Burundi, Rwanda and the Central African Republic, news outlets reported.

But, upon emergency appeal from the U.S. government, the U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to temporarily block the appeal court’s ruling and allow third-country deportations to continue — saying it will hear oral arguments in December and issue a final ruling then.

Attorneys advocating for Traore have filed a motion to stay her removal proceedings and contest her planned removal to Sierra Leone.

authors: Morgan Chilson, Baya Burgess, Anna Kaminski

text:
DODGE CITY — Southwest Kansas communities reeling from President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown — which included random stops to check status — are looking for ways to recover as fear continues to grip the area’s large Hispanic population.

Restaurants closed, motel managers cancelled reservations and the area’s large beef processing facilities shortened or called off shifts last week as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers rushed in and immigrant employees didn’t show up for work.

Breanna Rutschman, a Dodge City second grade teacher, said seven of her 20 students were absent the day the agents arrived. The next day, just eight students showed up. Other classrooms in the school were largely empty.

“They’re here to better their situation and improve the lives of their children, and they’re just hardworking and they’re caring and they’re human,” she said. “What’s happening is so inhumane and so cruel, and it’s unnecessary. It’s absolutely unnecessary.”

ICE agents arrived in the area Sept. 22, focusing immigration checks in Dodge City, Liberal and Garden City. The federal government reported making more than 100 arrests. Trump’s Department of Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin said through news releases that agents were arresting only “heinous criminals”

But on a list including murderers, rapists, and drug traffickers he added “illegal aliens with final orders of removal.” Mullin also said ICE agents, who work for Homeland Security, are not arresting people at worksites.

Local officials and advocates say that’s not what happened.

“It wasn’t just criminals, because I’ve been in contact with several schools, and I’ve been in contact with the families directly,” said Janeth Vazquez, vice mayor of Liberal. “The majority of these families did not have any criminal history. These were hardworking, humble, genuine, good people in our communities.”

Census data shows that Liberal, Dodge City and Garden City have populations ranging from 55% to 69% Hispanic or Latino.

As word of ICE’s presence spread, Vazquez said, Liberal became a “ghost town,” as people hid.

Federal officers arrested people after demanding proof of immigration status during traffic stops and from employees entering beef processing plants, and based on outstanding warrants, Vazaquez said.

“I’m not just talking about undocumented people. I’m talking about U.S. citizens as well,” she said. “They were racially profiling people and targeting people of color, and so all of those stories were shared across social media. People were terrified to leave their homes.”

Helping out

Amy Soberanes owns a small Dodge City shop selling juices and lattes. But since the ICE arrests she has another job: organizing a relief network to deliver food and other essentials to immigrants in hiding.

The front porch of Soberanes’ business was covered with donations in the days after the immigration searches. She gathered a team of driver-volunteers who go to homes to drop off diapers, baby formula, toilet paper and groceries, a community practice employed in Minneapolis, Los Angeles and other cities when ICE arrived.

The volunteers are careful, Soberanes said. Drivers switch routes and cars to avoid detection, and they write addresses on notebook paper and carry a water bottle so they can drop the paper in the water and obscure the addresses should they be stopped by authorities.

Last week, her phone rang constantly as she juggled boxes of diapers, bags of fruit and rolls of toilet paper.

“I have not slept the past three days,” she said Friday. “We have been out delivering food until midnight, and then getting up in the morning at 4 a.m. and delivering food before (ICE is) active from 8 a.m. to probably 6 p.m.”

Soberanes nonetheless said she was heartened by everyone who volunteered to help. Even cancellation of a long-planned Hispanic community event, the Pachanga en la Plaza, had a bright side, she said.

“What we are doing now is we have turned all the free food we were going to give out for the event, all the money we had gotten for it, and we are now donating it to the families,” Soberanes said.

Hurting, in hiding

In a small house, a family of seven crowded the living room last week, scared to leave and relying on donations dropped off by Soberanes.

A young woman, whom Kansas Reflector is not identifying because of her fear that ICE may retaliate against her and her family, cuddled her newborn son as she talked about her husband’s detention by ICE days earlier.

On Sept. 23, the woman and her husband were on the way home from the hospital with their newborn baby, she said in Spanish, speaking with help of a translator. Their doctor warned the couple to be careful as they traveled home because it was “dangerous” out there.

Despite precautions, they were stopped by ICE, and her husband was detained.

“The agents did have some mercy, but it was very little,” the woman said. “He let my kid and me go. One thing I am incredibly grateful for is that I am with my three kids here at home.”

The arrest happened near the couple’s house, she said, where her 4-year-old son came outside and saw her husband taken away.

“They didn’t care about my husband, and they just took him. I’m incredibly sad,” she said. Her husband immigrated to the United States with a work permit, but it wasn’t renewed.

“He appealed his case,” the woman said. “He did everything that was required of him. He came here legally. He did everything. They just didn’t renew it.”

An appeals court upheld a lower court’s decision that asylum and an application for protection under the Convention Against Torture were not appropriate for him, court records confirm. The court decided that the man’s refusal to join criminal gangs in Guatemala was not sufficient to show his life was endangered, and that his race didn’t play a role in his fear of specific “actors” in his birth country.

“His lawyer at the time told him just stay where you’re at and just don’t do anything,” the woman said. “So he didn’t know what to do. We feel like that lawyer didn’t help us at all that time, but we didn’t know much at the moment, so we just let it go.”

The woman said she spoke on the phone to her husband days after agents took him. He said he was being held in San Diego but expected to be deported to Guatemala.

She said she doesn’t see how she can return to Guatemala.

“I can’t because of my kids. I need to take care of my kids. They have a future here,” she said. “In Guatemala, there is no future. We don’t have a house there. We don’t have anything.”

The couple’s current attorney said she can’t help anymore because she can’t get in contact with the husband, the woman said.

The young woman dissolved into quiet tears when she talked about her husband. “He hasn’t done anything. He doesn’t drink. He plays in the church band. These were the last words that he told me: ‘Take care of yourself. Take care of our kids.’”

Volunteers, including three attorneys who are working pro bono with southwest Kansas immigrants, will coordinate with the man to help him apply to return, Soberanes said. The family was unsure if he signed a stipulation agreement while in detention, a form commonly used with immigrant detainees in which they agree to be deported without going through immigration court, according to the National Immigration Project.

The man was the breadwinner for his family of seven, which includes his wife and their three children, his own mother, and his younger brother, who is deaf.

Protesting ICE

In response to ICE’s presence, hundreds of people lined Dodge City’s signature downtown plaza with its life-sized bronze Texas longhorn steer on Sept. 24, waving flags from Mexico, Guatemala and the United States.

They carried signs urging kindness and cursing ICE.

The following day, protesters marched from Wright Park to U.S. Republican Rep. Tracey Mann’s Dodge City office, where the doors were locked before the demonstrators arrived. Mann represents Kansas’ vast 1st Congressional District, which stretches some 400 miles east to west, from Lawrence to the border with Colorado.

Mann did not answer Kansas Reflector questions submitted by email about why the office was closed or whether he was concerned by disruptions to Kansas businesses.

“Federal law enforcement has a responsibility to enforce our immigration laws and help keep our communities safe,” Mann said in an emailed statement. “I also recognize the disruption the operation caused for communities across the Big First. When possible, federal authorities should coordinate with local law enforcement so operations can be carried out safely.”

Complications of gaining citizenship

Not all of those in southwest Kansas are sympathetic about the ICE raids.

Residents commented under social media posts telling immigrants to simply file paperwork to gain legal status or leave, and thanking ICE for their work, even as others mourned families torn apart.

But attaining citizenship isn’t as easy as it may sound.

In 2011, Ana Sanchez Ortiz’s stepfather petitioned for her, along with her siblings and mother, to become U.S. citizens.

Fifteen years later, Sanchez Ortiz’s mother still isn’t a citizen, and on Sept. 23, she was detained. That was despite checking in for years with ICE, holding a job at National Beef Packing Co. and staying out of trouble, Sanchez Ortiz said.

Sanchez Ortiz, a senior branch manager at a Dodge City bank, hesitated at first to speak out, fearful of drawing attention.

But frantic family members couldn’t find her mother in the federal detention system for several days, she said. Her mother is diabetic and has high blood pressure, and although Sanchez Ortiz’s sister rushed her medications to the local jail, ICE agents wouldn’t give it to her mother.

The family now know their mother is being detained in California, and they have traveled there to try to help her, Sanchez Ortiz said.

“We have done everything the right way. She’s been here since she was 16 years old,” Sanchez Ortiz said. “She went to high school here. She started her family here.”

Because she came to the country when she was 4 years old, Sanchez Ortiz became a citizen through the DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, program. This Obama-era immigration policy allows certain immigrants who were brought to the United States as children to receive renewable two-year work permits

She renewed her DACA application six times before she could apply for the separate status of legal residency, which she received when she was a freshman in high school. But it wasn’t until she was 31 years old that she became a citizen, Sanchez Ortiz said.

Looking for a solution

Zac Carlton owns a construction company in Dodge City, and he said friends were “gutted” by ICE activities last week. Everyone in the area knows someone who is not here legally, he said.

“I’ve talked to multiple contractors and subcontractors, and everybody was laying low last week, and no work was getting done,” he said. “Now this week, people are trying to figure out how to recover. It has put a strain on, obviously, the families that were affected by the sweep, and then the employers.”

Western Kansas needs immigrants to support construction, agriculture and other businesses, Carlton said. Finding workers is already an issue in those industries, he said, and will continue to be so.

Carlton looked at past immigration laws and policies and is circulating a petition to promote the SEAL Act, which stands for secure, earned, accountable and lawful, he said.

Immigration reform bills have failed multiple times in the past, he said, but he’s hopeful politicians will pay attention after what happened in Kansas.

Vazquez has been fighting the battle Carlton is attempting for about 15 years, traveling to Washington, D.C., to advocate for immigration changes. She began when her father was deported right as she started college as a teenager. Five years ago, she became a Liberal city commissioner, the first Latina in the position.

What happened in Southwest Kansas last week will reverberate across the nation because of the effects on the beef supply, she said. Industry groups raised concerns that employees who skipped work at beef processing facilities for fear of encountering ICE could contribute to slowed production and higher prices.

“This whole operation just truly put an impact on our economy, and everybody in Southwest Kansas is going to suffer,” Vazquez said, “not just the undocumented population.”

title: 'We had to step up': Santa Fe councilors bar ICE staging on city property
authors: Carina Julig, Jim Weber, New Mexican file photo, Nathan Burton
description: A legal resident from Guatemala was detained by ICE for 23 days after being arrested while taking his daughter to a medical appointment, highlighting fears of immigration enforcement in Santa
text:
Demonstrators gather for a protest at Roundhouse on Aug. 20 against a surge of recent ICE arrests stoking an environment of fear for some local immigrants. Following at least 15 ICE arrests in Santa Fe that month, the City Council on Wednesday approved new legislation prohibiting the use of city property for federal immigration enforcement purposes.

Edgar Chacon-Miranda, a legal resident, spent 23 days in an immigration detention facility after he was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers while taking one of his daughters to a medical appointment.

On Wednesday, the 45-year-old Guatemalan immigrant urged the Santa Fe City Council to try to prevent other families from experiencing what his went through.

“The emotional impact that these experiences give our children is lasting,” he said in Spanish through an interpreter. “Places that should be safe havens have instead become sources of constant fear. We should not have to go through what happened to me.”

Chacon-Miranda, who became the face of rising ICE activity in Santa Fe after his high-profile arrest Aug. 19 in the parking lot of a medical clinic, was one of many people who spoke before the council unanimously passed an ordinance prohibiting the use of city property for immigration enforcement purposes.

“No child should have to go to school, should have to go to their doctor, should have to go to bed at night, wondering if they’re not going to see their parents again,” said Councilor Paul Bustamante, who sponsored the ordinance along with Mayor Michael Garcia and Councilors Liz Barrett, Alma Castro and Pilar Faulkner.

The ordinance prohibits city-owned property including parking lots, parks or vacant lots from being used for immigration enforcement purposes, “including as a staging area, processing location or operations base.”

The ordinance also requires businesses to notify employees if they are required to complete an I-9 audit, a federal inspection of whether workers are legally eligible to work in the U.S.

At the meeting, the council’s one Republican, Lee Garcia, clarified the ordinance does not stop federal agents from conducting operations in Santa Fe — it just prohibits them from using city property to do so. As one of the councilors representing Santa Fe’s immigrant-heavy south side, he noted he represents many of the people who have said they are now living in fear due to rising ICE activity.

“By no means do I feel like with this we’re advocating for anyone to break the law, but I do feel we do have to stand for individuals who are fearful of persecution,” he said.

The Santa Fe County Commission passed a similar ordinance Tuesday regarding county property.

“Public safety cannot mean safety for some and fear for others,” District 2 Commissioner Lisa Cacari-Stone said in a statement. “When one of us is not safe, none of us are safe.”

City Attorney Marcos Martinez said the city’s ordinance was inspired by legislation adopted by Albuquerque earlier this year, which led the U.S. Department of Justice to add the city to a lawsuit against the state of New Mexico challenging regulations prohibiting state and local government cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Bernalillo and Doña Ana counties are also parties to the lawsuit.

Martinez said local governments have the authority to regulate their own property, similar to how a private citizen could ask to be shown a warrant before allowing law enforcement to enter their home or business.

“Based off of the other jurisdictions where this issue has been decided, I believe that the city of Albuquerque will prevail,” he said. “For similar reasons, I think our ordinance would be defensible.”

Santa Fe resident Edgar Chacon-Miranda, second from right, stands in the street of his neighborhood with his three daughters, from left, Emilia Aleysha Chacon, 11, Jaylah Areli Chacon, 13, Dora Elisa Chacon, 2, on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. Chacon-Miranda was arrested by federal immigration agents in August and is free after 23 days in Torrance County Detention Center. His lawyers allege his arrest was wrongful and immigration agents lied on sworn affidavits.

Despite the risk of a federal lawsuit, Barrett said she felt the city had a duty to respond to the community members urging them to act.

“You’re brave to come here and come speak here tonight, and we had to step up too and be brave,” she said.

More than a dozen people spoke about the ordinance, including former Santa Fe Mayor David Coss, who described immigrants as “productive members of our community living their lives.”

“I never thought I’d be in a country where people disappear, as if we were Chile or Argentina in the 1980s,” he said. “States have rights too, and municipalities have rights too, and I want to encourage you to pass this and protect the rights of everyone in this community.”

Only one person who spoke was not in support of the measure, a man who frequently and loudly insults councilors during public comment periods and refuses to provide his name. He described the ordinance as “pandering” and accused the council of trying to obstruct justice.

“This ordinance means nothing to federal agents,” he said. “If federal agents wanted to come in this door right now, they can come in here and arrest all the illegals.”

Several people said they were speaking on behalf of others who supported the proposal but were afraid to come.

Marcela Gonzales spoke about her family’s experience immigrating from Mexico in the 1980s and becoming small business owners in Santa Fe.

“We’re not all criminals, and we deserve to be treated as humans,” she said, expressing support for the ordinance.

The ordinance was introduced in September at the same time as two other measures related to immigration policy. One would reaffirm the city’s existing legislation in support of immigrants, encouraging residents to rely on the city’s public safety services and “encouraging all community members and community leaders to fact-check public safety information.” The second would update the city Immigration Committee’s guidelines to include a member of the City Council and a designated police department liaison.

Both were postponed at last week’s City Council Quality of Life committee meeting in order for councilors to have more time to introduce and discuss amendments. They are currently scheduled for a final vote later in October.

title: Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely
description:
For nearly a year, the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, has been Adam’s prison.
It was only midway through the 13 hour and 10 minute flight that they found out – while shackled – that they were headed toward Equatorial Guinea.
Since then, the US government has forcibly transferred at least 65 third country nationals to Equatorial Guinea.
Yet one by one, Equatorial Guinea has been sending them back to harm in the very places from which they fled.
In Equatorial Guinea, it is also fueling the corruption and impunity our organizations have spent decades documenting and countering.
text:
For nearly a year, the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, has been Adam’s prison. He is confined alone to a hotel room, under constant watch by the security officers and soldiers of a notoriously oppressive regime who control his movements. Not long ago, they barged into his room, handcuffed and beat him, and warned him not to tell anyone. There is no cell to point to, no charges or formal sentence, and nothing on paper to document his plight.

Adam, 26, has chosen not to share his real name or even his country of origin out of fear for his safety. He fled indefinite, forced military conscription in his home country after enduring abuse during his military service.

Adam sought safety in the United States. A US immigration judge heard his case, found that he would probably face persecution if forced to return to his country of origin, and issued a formal order shielding him from removal there. Then, in November 2025, the United States sent him to Equatorial Guinea, a country he had never set foot in and where torture reportedly occurs in every prison nationwide, according to the most recent state department human rights report. Adam, and the other men onboard the flight, were told they were being transferred to another US detention facility. It was only midway through the 13 hour and 10 minute flight that they found out – while shackled – that they were headed toward Equatorial Guinea.

None of this is happening in a vacuum. In November, the Trump administration repurposed $7.5m to pay the government of Equatorial Guinea to accept third country nationals from the United States, a 275% foreign assistance increase and departure from longstanding US policy against direct provision of aid to a deeply corrupt and abusive regime. Congress appropriated these taxpayer funds for humanitarian assistance for refugees in dire need – money that is now used to detain, shackle and eventually send refugees back to the countries they fled. Since then, the US government has forcibly transferred at least 65 third country nationals to Equatorial Guinea. US immigration judges had granted protection to nearly all of these individuals due to the high risk of persecution or torture they face in their countries of origin. Yet one by one, Equatorial Guinea has been sending them back to harm in the very places from which they fled.

In the past few weeks, in retaliation for speaking out against the detention conditions and police violence, police in Equatorial Guinea violently assaulted and arrested two of the refugees, witnesses and lawyers say, including Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian man from Arizona who has lived in the United States since he was three years old, and Samson Birhane. Today, they remain in police custody, detained incommunicado.

This is part of an escalating scheme by the Trump administration to send immigrants and refugees to countries around the world where they have no connection and often face grave harm. In Equatorial Guinea, it is also fueling the corruption and impunity our organizations have spent decades documenting and countering.

Equatorial Guinea’s government and ruling family are, by any measure, among the most corrupt on earth. About a decade ago, the US justice department settled a civil forfeiture case against the country’s vice-president, Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, or “Teodorín”. He forfeited a $30m Malibu mansion, a Ferrari and Michael Jackson memorabilia.

Some governments have rightly taken serious action to restrain Teodorín’s corruption, such as the sanctions the UK government imposed on him in 2021. Yet last September, the Trump administration did the opposite, and quietly paused corruption-related visa restrictions that had prevented Teodorín from traveling to the United States, clearing the way for him to meet with Christopher Landau, the US deputy secretary of state, before the deal to accept non-Equatoguineans removed from the United States.

In addition to these funds, the deal affords Teodorin something he has long sought: legitimacy and access in Washington DC.

We are seeing that access to US policymakers deepening in real time. Last week, Teodorín was back in New York, meeting with Landau again, this time at the United Nations, where they celebrated what the government of Equatorial Guinea referred to as a positive evolution of the bilateral relationship. They discussed expanding cooperation beyond energy to banking, trade investment, security and diplomacy.

Our organizations have worked for years to demand accountability for rampant corruption in Equatorial Guinea, and now, to fight for the refugees and torture victims being unlawfully sent there. After building the evidentiary dossier that led to UK sanctions, EG Justice is now challenging Equatorial Guinea’s participation in the US deportation scheme before the African Commission on People’s and Human Rights, while working with local attorneys to offer legal and humanitarian aid. In July, the African Commission on Human and People’s rights issued an emergency ruling, ordering the government of Equatorial Guinea not to send people back to danger in their home country – a ruling that the government has ignored since, sending four people back to the very places from which they had sought, and received, protection.

Human Rights First (HRF), for its part, together with partner organizations, successfully challenged the third-country deportation policy in federal court, but the US supreme court has since intervened to allow these rapid third-country deportations to resume while it rules on the case. HRF also leads the ICE Flight Monitor platform, uncovering in real time hidden deportation flights to Equatorial Guinea and beyond, while partnering with Refugees International to shed light on proliferating and often opaque US third-country forced transfer agreements with 35 countries.

Time is of the essence, as Adam has been sick with malaria and typhoid fever since November. His second asylum claim, filed with Equatoguinean authorities in January, remains in indefinite limbo. The judge in the case told local counsel that he does not have authority to hear it, as the vice-president is in charge of these cases. The habeas corpus petition his lawyer filed also remains unanswered. Guards tell him repeatedly to “go back to your country,” the very outcome a US judge already ruled would put him at high risk of persecution.

There is a clearcut, fair, and humane path forward. We are pressing for coordinated Magnitsky-style sanctions against senior Equatoguinean officials, including Teodorín, in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union simultaneously, building on the evidentiary dossier the UK relied on in 2021. In the United States, Congress must exercise fully its oversight authority to end misappropriation of migration and refugee resettlement funds to finance arbitrary detention and chain refoulement – and, in effect, to reward torturers.

Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them, or returned to live safely in the United States. They deserve the protection that was promised to them and is enshrined in US and international law.

title: Federal funds for local police enforcement accelerated Trump immigration crackdown
description:
An unprecedented increase in cooperation between local and state law enforcement and federal immigration officers through collaborations known as 287(g) agreements helped drive numbers up.
The agreements allow state and local law enforcement agencies to enforce parts of federal immigration law and have become an arm of Trump’s mass deportation campaign.
ICE does not distinguish between arrests initially made by local law enforcement or federal officials.
Local law enforcement officers under this model do not inquire about immigration status.
Local governments that have not wanted to participate in federal immigration enforcement have been dubbed sanctuary cities.
text:
WASHINGTON — This summer, arrests of immigrants in the United States soared to the highest levels since President Donald Trump returned to office.

An unprecedented increase in cooperation between local and state law enforcement and federal immigration officers through collaborations known as 287(g) agreements helped drive numbers up.

The agreements allow state and local law enforcement agencies to enforce parts of federal immigration law and have become an arm of Trump’s mass deportation campaign. Republicans in Congress have provided billions in federal funding for local departments that accept the agreements, creating a deluge of new partners.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, a senior Department of Homeland Security official during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, said the billions in new funding has helped the program grow.

“Mostly, 287(g) agreements were voluntary, and the costs were borne by the state and local government to train their own people,” she said. “Now, the federal government has money to pay them, and so that's encouraging more states and localities to do it because it's a budget plus-up.”

In June, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded roughly 43,000 immigration arrests, followed by 49,000 in July and nearly 51,000 in August. ICE does not distinguish between arrests initially made by local law enforcement or federal officials.

Those three months also saw the most new 287(g) agreements signed since Trump took office, according to a States Newsroom analysis of government data.

“ICE has increased efforts with state and local law enforcement to assist federal immigration officers in our efforts to make America safe again,” a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement to States Newsroom.

But those efforts have generated protests in some of the communities where they’ve appeared.

Democrats in Maryland and Maine passed laws restricting cooperation between local police and ICE. The Maryland measure’s supporters said it would reduce distrust of police.

Skyrocketing growth

The president's signature 2025 domestic policy bill, the “One, Big Beautiful” Act, set aside about $4 billion for state and local governments to conduct immigration enforcement, including 287(g) programs. The Secure America Act passed in June allocated more than $31 billion to implement those agreements as well.

Both packages were passed by Republicans through a legislative maneuver known as reconciliation that did not need Democratic votes.

The funds incentivized massive growth.

Before Trump took office in January 2025, the federal government had agreements with 135 state and local police departments. As of Oct. 1, those agreements skyrocketed to 2,608, according to DHS data.

Local departments or state agencies in 38 states have 287(g) agreements, with the highest numbers in Texas and Florida, where there are state laws requiring local law enforcement to partake in the program.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday the Florida Highway Patrol was eligible for $26 million in reimbursements from the federal government for arrests from April through June.

“My educated guess would be that a large number of the arrests and detentions that we've seen increasing in recent months in the summer were because there was an increase in 287(g) agreements in Texas and Florida, but other parts of the country as well,” said Ariel G. Ruiz Soto, a senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a think tank that studies global migration.

ICE does not always specify when an immigration arrest is made through the partnership program, but the Deportation Data Project, a project of the University of California schools in Berkeley and Los Angeles that analyzes government immigration enforcement data, has attributed at least 6,150 arrests in July, about 12.5% of all arrests for that month.

Only 12 states have no such agreements. They are California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington state.

Three models

The partnership program was created in a 1996 law, but not actively used until the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It first received federal appropriations in 2006.

Three types of partnerships operate within the program.

The loosest type of agreement is the jail enforcement model, where deputized officers can inquire about the immigration status of people arrested on state or local charges, as well as hold a noncitizen for ICE to pick up for up to 48 hours.

In another model, the warrants service officer model, ICE trains, certifies and allows state and local law enforcement to issue administrative warrants, which are not signed by a judge, but by an ICE official requesting the arrest of a noncitizen. Local law enforcement officers under this model do not inquire about immigration status.

The task force model, which involves the greatest immigration enforcement by local officers, allows for immigration officials to deputize local officers to partake in immigration duties such as asking about immigration status or even detaining people and transferring them to ICE.

As part of its immigration crackdown, the second Trump administration revived the task force model after the Obama administration discontinued it in 2012 over concerns of racial profiling.

It has seen the largest increase under Trump, Ruiz Soto said.

More than 71% of 287(g) agreements now use the task force model, according to Titus Consulting, a firm that tracks the agreements. About 7% use the jail enforcement model and more than 21% use the warrant model.

The task force model is “hands down,” the most effective method in arresting noncitizens, said Todd Bensmen, a senior research fellow for the Border Security and Immigration Center at The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank.

“If they're not deputized under that, they just come into contact with people that are fully … deportable, and then just leave them be,” he said of local law enforcement. “They can just arrest them on the spot and call ICE, and that way you have a really dramatic force multiplier and ICE doesn't have to do anything but come and pick them up.”

Program changes

In 2006, the Bush administration took an interest in exploring 287(g) programs, specifically the jail enforcement model because it was easy for ICE to identify people who are subject to an immigration arrest, said Brown.

“If your job is to find people, wow, that's the easiest thing to do,” she said of the jail model.

Brown said that spurred the idea for the Secure Communities program. Under the program, the FBI automatically sent fingerprints of a person booked in custody to DHS to check against its immigration database. If the person was a noncitizen who was unauthorized in the U.S., then ICE was notified.

The program was voluntary, but there was pushback from immigration advocates during the Obama administration, Brown said.

“There was a concern that this was mixing criminal enforcement and immigration enforcement in ways they weren't meant to, (and) it was creating fear among immigration communities of reporting crimes for fear that they would be arrested,” she said.

The Obama administration pulled back and redirected the Secure Communities program to a federal government model.

“They turned it from like a community-by-community rollout to just a federal-to-federal information sharing agreement that remains in place today,” she said.

Brown said the difference now is that some communities have decided when ICE is notified, if at all, and whether or not to honor detainers, which are requests from ICE to hold an immigrant until federal immigration officers arrive.

Local governments that have not wanted to participate in federal immigration enforcement have been dubbed sanctuary cities.

The Trump administration has threatened to pull federal funding from those cities that don’t want to aid in immigration enforcement and has offered an influx of cash to states and local governments that have agreed to participate.

The Republican Congress has funded the program for the next three years, Ruiz Soto noted.

“It would then come to … what a future administration or a future Congress would do to continue expanding this or not fulfill them anymore,” he said. “But clearly right now ICE has significant funding to last for 287(g) and much more other enforcement in the near future.”

description:
Attorneys for the family of Renee Good have filed two civil lawsuits Thursday against the United States, federal agents and members of the Trump administration after she was shot and killed during an immigration operation in Minneapolis.
RELATED: What we know about Renee Good, the mother of 3 killed by ICE agent in Minneapolis One of the cases names the United States as a defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act.
The lawsuits said Renee stopped her car on Portland Avenue and honked her horn to alert neighbors about the presence of federal agents.
Becca Good, Renee’s partner, got out to record a video while Renee stayed in the driver’s seat.
Attorneys for the family argued Ross and other federal agents violated Department of Homeland Security use-of-force policies.
text:
Attorneys for the family of Renee Good have filed two civil lawsuits Thursday against the United States, federal agents and members of the Trump administration after she was shot and killed during an immigration operation in Minneapolis.

Chicago-based law firm Romanucci & Blandin filed the lawsuits in connection with the Jan. 7 shooting during Operation Metro Surge.

RELATED: What we know about Renee Good, the mother of 3 killed by ICE agent in Minneapolis

One of the cases names the United States as a defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The lawsuit alleges wrongful death, assault, negligence and other claims.

A second lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to violate civil rights and names federal agents and several current and former federal officials: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross, who shot Good; former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem; White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Border Patrol Commander at Large Gregory Bovino; Corey Lewandowski, a former special government employee working within Homeland Security; former Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons; White House border czar Tom Homan; and 10 unnamed federal agents.

What do the lawsuits claim?

The lawsuits said Renee stopped her car on Portland Avenue and honked her horn to alert neighbors about the presence of federal agents. Becca Good, Renee’s partner, got out to record a video while Renee stayed in the driver’s seat.

The lawsuit claims Renee then began to pull forward slowly after turning the vehicle’s wheels away from Ross.

Then, Ross moved out of the vehicle’s path, then fired one shot through the windshield and two more through the open driver’s side window. One bullet struck Renee in the head, and she was later pronounced dead at a nearby hospital.

“Not a single shot was justified,” attorney Antonio Romanucci said.

The firm said no agent gave medical aid after the shooting. It said a bystander who identified himself as a physician offered help, but an agent turned him away.

Attorneys for the family argued Ross and other federal agents violated Department of Homeland Security use-of-force policies.

“Renee had the right to speak, express herself, assemble, observe, and leave the scene unharmed and alive,” Romanucci said.

Family members shared about Renee’s legacy, describing her as a good mother and person. Becca spoke in public for the first time since Renee’s death, calling her the love of her life.

“True accountability and change is the only way to make sure no other family has to go through what we have,” Becca said.

‘Every morning, she is my first thought.’

“She was the center of my universe, and living without her is like trying to live without the sun,” said Becca. “And you don’t know how much light something gives you until it’s gone, and you feel that absence every single second.”

Becca says Renee was a writer, a poet and a loving mother to her three kids.

“Her youngest, our son, is 6 years old, and he’s already lost more than anyone ever should, and he missed his mama,” she said quietly. “He misses her hugs and her laughs and her jokes, and he misses her singing.”

Also speaking Thursday was Renee’s brother Brent Ganger, who said he and his family want to honor her life with a kinder, more civil America. Ganger explained that his family’s beliefs are across the political spectrum.

“Renee was the first and loudest person to root for you, and Renee exuded light, and that light has been extinguished,” Ganger said. “I want to say very clearly that despite our differences, our family members all love each other very much, deeply.”

Becca says she wants accountability and understanding from those responsible for her partner’s death, to understand the pain of their loss.

“Every morning, she is my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” Becca said.

“We are here today, not out of anger and not out of hate. We are here because Renee’s love and legacy demand a better world, for her children, for this community, and for this country.”

text:
AUSTIN — A Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot by a federal immigration agent in Texas had surgery Thursday to remove the bullet lodged in his back for nearly two weeks.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, had appeared in court in a wheelchair on Wednesday, wearing a sling on his arm. He remains in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest.

Garces Perez struck an officer with his side mirror on Sept. 20 while trying to drive away, authorities said. The federal officer who shot Garces Perez, and who allegedly was hit by the side mirror of Garces Perez’s car, wasn’t wearing a body camera.

Garces Perez faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted on the assault charge.

The bullet was successfully removed during surgery, and Garces Perez is recovering in the custody of the U.S. Marshalls, said Fabiana Melendez Ruiz, a spokesperson for his legal team.

His case has sparked outrage and protests in the Texas capital city against President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, including agents’ conduct.

Garces Perez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garces Perez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the officer fired his weapon.

Footage provided Wednesday in court shows officers pulling over Garces Perez in Austin, where he was delivering food for DoorDash.

text:
Two people detained outside a Chicago-area immigration detention center last year are suing right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson for defamation, saying he falsely portrayed them as violent extremists who assaulted federal officers.

Illinois residents Kyle Frankovich, a data scientist at Harvard University, and Maureen Foody, a contract court reporter, filed the lawsuit Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. They said they were detained while protesting peacefully outside the Broadview detention center, but that Johnson knowingly framed them as criminals and “left-wing terrorists” in videos he posted to millions of viewers.

It appears to be the first defamation suit related to the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown filed against a member of the administration’s unofficial team of MAGA influencers, a corps of creators who amplify the government’s framing of left-wing protesters as dangerous agitators in exchange for access that draws online audiences and shapes the conservative news cycle.

Karianne Jones, a lawyer at Evergreen Legal Strategies, one of the firms representing Frankovich and Foody, told MS NOW that the lawsuit is a way to hold accountable people who “serve as a mouthpiece for the government.”

Johnson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Johnson, a former conservative writer for BuzzFeed who was fired for plagiarism, remade himself as a right-wing activist, creating content for Turning Point USA and then his own online video channels. He is one of several creators the second Trump administration has leaned on to promote its narratives and celebrate its agenda. In 2025, Johnson was invited to sit in a special “new media” seat in the White House briefing room and brought on ride-alongs with Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials. He was part of a gaggle of influencers given special access to document ICE operations and anti-ICE protests, who parroted Trump administration claims that left-wing domestic terrorists were waging a nationwide campaign of violence against federal agents.

The lawsuit described Johnson’s content as “political combat dressed up as news.”

On Oct. 3, 2025, Johnson accompanied then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino to the Broadview ICE facility, which had become a site of escalating confrontations between agents and the citizens, journalists and local politicians who gathered there to protest the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign in Chicago and the conditions inside the jail. Videos from outside Broadview had gone viral, showing agents shoving protesters and firing tear gas and pepper balls, seemingly without justification.

Frankovich and Foody were among the crowd of protesters the day that Johnson arrived. They were standing in a designated “free speech” zone, when — without provocation, according to the complaint — several protestors were shoved, struck, forced to the ground and detained by agents.

In an interview with MS NOW, Frankovich said he had come out to support his community, as he and his wife had done for weeks — handing out whistles, providing security for families at schools and showing up at Broadview.

The documentary-style videos Johnson posted to X, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram and Rumble show the podcaster seemingly taunting the protestors as federal agents stood between them.

“These are exactly the kind of people that we want to be pissing off … It’s your tears that keep us going,” Johnson says in one.

In the next scene, Johnson shows around 10 detained protesters, including Frankovich and Foody, lined up along a guardrail outside the Broadview detention center, their hands bound by zip ties. He refers to them as “left-wing terrorists arrested for attacking police officers and ICE officers.”

“All of this was false, which Mr. Johnson knew,” the complaint says.

“I saw dozens of Democrat domestic terrorists arrested today for VIOLENT ASSAULT on federal law enforcement. Every activist here attacked ICE agents in broad daylight just for enforcing American law,” Johnson captioned one of many videos from that day posted to X.

The post was viewed 1.7 million times and drew hundreds of comments calling the detained protesters “domestic terrorists” and calling for their deportation and prosecution. Johnson shared at least seven posts about his day at Broadview, which garnered millions of collective views.

Frankovich and Foody were not charged with any crime. After being detained for around eight hours, which Frankovich described as traumatizing, they were released without charges a half-mile from the jail, according to the complaint.

After his release, Frankovich said he was shaken when he saw Johnson’s posts and the comments that followed. He said Johnson’s audience was calling him an antifa leader, speculating about his identity and “trying to find me and stop me.” Comments in the complaint included calls to torture, shoot and kill the detained protestors.

More articles

DHS turned a photo of Frankovich being detained into a recruitment poster.

“FAFO” — short for “fuck around and find out,” an acronym popular with the far right — the DHS caption read, above a photo of Frankovich, his distinctive tattoos visible, in zip ties.

“We will NOT allow violent activist [sic] to lay hands on our law enforcement,” it continued.

Below the photo it said: “JOIN.ICE.GOV.”

Frankovich is also one of dozens of U.S. citizens and legal residents who have filed recent complaints to DHS over Operation Midway Blitz, alleging immigration agents used excessive force and detained people illegally, among other harms.

title: Ola Bini Ordered to Leave Ecuador Under Obscure Accusations
description:
The ground for deportation is a secret report which allegedly asserts that Bini committed acts against the security of Ecuador.
Ola Bini was relocated to Quito's airport and must stay there until fly back to Sweden.
Yesterday's events open a new chapter in the nefarious persecution of Ola Bini by Ecuadorean authorities.
In a case surrounded by political interests, Ola Bini’s unanimous acquittal by the lower court in 2023 was overturned after the prosecution’s appeal.
Ecuadorean authorities must explain the accusations against the security expert.
text:
In a new blow to Ola Bini’s legal guarantees, Ecuadorean authorities retained the free software developer and security expert yesterday in Quito and ordered his immediate deportation from the country. He is barred from returning to Ecuador for 10 years.

According to information released by his lawyer, Bini was intercepted by a car with four people who identified themselves as immigration agents. He was then taken to an immigration office without further information or a formal order from a competent authority. There, officials told Bini that his visa had been revoked but didn’t show any supporting document.

Bini's defense filed a habeas corpus to safeguard his freedom and prevent his deportation. Yet, Ecuadorian authorities affirmed that the developer represents a threat or risk to public security and the state structure, and must leave the country. The ground for deportation is a secret report which allegedly asserts that Bini committed acts against the security of Ecuador. The defense could not access its contents.

The deportation hearing started yesterday at 5pm Quito time. Human rights organizations tried to attend the hearing but were denied entry. The hearing was suspended but later reinstalled establishing his immediate deportation. Ola Bini was relocated to Quito's airport and must stay there until fly back to Sweden.

The case that led to Bini's unfounded criminal conviction has expired (the statute of limitations ran out) and the court had already formally lifted all precautionary measures against him. Yesterday's events open a new chapter in the nefarious persecution of Ola Bini by Ecuadorean authorities.

Since Bini’s arbitrary arrest in 2019, EFF has reported about his criminal prosecution fraught with misconceptions and rights violations. The script of what happened yesterday follows the same patterns we saw in the entire case, from its outset with unjustified allegations that Bini was a national security risk. The Observation Mission of Ola Bini’s case, joined by EFF and other digital and human rights organizations, has published reports and raised international awarenness about the perils of this case to the protection of rights online and the beneficial work of security experts.

In a case surrounded by political interests, Ola Bini’s unanimous acquittal by the lower court in 2023 was overturned after the prosecution’s appeal. The majority of the appeals court convicted Bini for attempted unauthorized access of a telecommunications system without actual evidence to corroborate the accusation claims.

Now, once again we must sound the alarm. Ecuadorean authorities must explain the accusations against the security expert. We will remain vigilant and ensure that at least this time his rights are respected.

text:
Oct 2 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court is hearing a series of important cases during its new term that begins on ⁠Monday ⁠involving issues such as President Donald Trump's immigration policies, assault-style rifle ⁠bans, Big Oil's financial liability for climate change, Republican-backed voting restrictions, LGBT rights and more.

Here is a look at some of the cases being argued during the ​term, which runs to about the end of June.

TRUMP'S MANDATORY IMMIGRATION DETENTION

The court will decide the legality of Trump's policy that subjects millions of immigrants in the US illegally to mandatory detention during deportation proceedings. The policy is part of Trump's pursuit ‌of mass deportation. The justices took up the Trump administration's ‌appeal of a lower court's ruling against the policy in a case involving a Brazilian national. The administration abandoned the US government's longstanding interpretation of federal law that immigrants already living in the US could be released on bond while their ⁠cases play out in immigration ⁠court. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

TRUMP'S THIRD-COUNTRY ​DEPORTATIONS

The justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own — so-called "third countries" — without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. The court on September 29 let the administration continue the policy for the time being, putting on hold a federal judge's ruling that removing migrants to third countries is unlawful. More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy, according to human rights groups. A ruling is expected by ​the end of June.

BAN ON ASSAULT-STYLE RIFLES

The justices will hear arguments on December 2 in a challenge to the legality of state prohibitions on assault-style rifles, giving them another chance to expand gun rights ⁠in ⁠a case that involves a type of weapon ⁠often associated with mass shootings. Lower courts upheld ​bans in Cook County, Illinois, and Connecticut on powerful semiautomatic rifles such as AR-15s. The lower courts rejected arguments that the measures violate the US Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and ​bear arms." Gun rights groups and other challengers have said that ⁠Supreme Court precedents concerning the Second Amendment protect these firearms, which they described as in "common use." A ruling is expected by the end of June.

BIG OIL CLIMATE SUIT

The court will hear arguments on Monday in a bid by ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to scuttle a lawsuit brought by officials in Boulder, Colorado, that seeks to hold the oil companies liable for helping drive climate change. The companies appealed after a lower court let the litigation move forward. The suit alleging state law violations by the companies seeks unspecified monetary damages for costs incurred by Boulder associated with mitigating the impact of climate change. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

VOTING RIGHTS

The justices will hear arguments on December 8 in a Republican-led bid ⁠to revive voter restrictions in Arizona that would stiffen proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registrants and purge state voter rolls of alleged non-US citizens. Republicans appealed after a ⁠lower court halted provisions of Arizona's law because they were found to violate a federal voting registration statute. President Donald Trump's administration has backed key elements of the appeal. Critics have said the Arizona measure adds extra mandates for voting that unfairly target Latino, Native American and student voters. Those groups tend to favor Democratic candidates. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

LGBT RIGHTS

The justices will hear arguments on November 3 in a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver and other Catholic entities to be exempted from a Colorado preschool funding program's nondiscrimination requirement. A lower court found that Colorado's program did not violate the religious rights of the Catholic plaintiffs under the US Constitution's First Amendment. The program provides state funds for preschools. The Catholic plaintiffs objected to the state's requirement that schools receiving funding under the program give all children "equal opportunity" to enroll in preschool regardless of certain characteristics, including the sexual orientation or gender identity of students or their family members. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

EPIC GAMES SUIT AGAINST APPLE

The justices will hear Apple's bid to escape being found in contempt in its legal fight with "Fortnite" maker Epic Games after the iPhone maker was deemed in ⁠violation of a judicial order mandating sweeping changes to its lucrative App Store in the antitrust litigation. Apple appealed a lower court's ruling upholding a decision by an Oakland, California-based federal judge finding Apple in contempt in Epic's 2020 lawsuit contesting App Store fees. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

PEPSICO TRADEMARK CASE

The court will hear arguments in a bid by canned-coffee maker Rise Brewing to hold PepsiCo liable for alleged trademark infringement concerning Pepsi's morning energy drink "Mtn Dew Rise." Rise appealed a lower court's ruling rejecting the company's ​claim that the product name "Mtn Dew Rise" infringes its trademarks and creates customer confusion with its coffee brand. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ​ruling is expected by the end of June.

(Compliled by Andrew Chung and John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

text:
Within the past 24 hours, federal immigration agents were told to change two of their tactics for targeting alleged illegal immigrants in recent days, with a judge seeking to end detentions outside immigration court and ICE's executive associate director issuing a policy memo altering traffic stops.

The changes could have a major effect on how agents target those in the U.S. without legal status, but who do not necessarily have criminal records, with ICE having heavily targeted immigration courts where immigrants are facing hearings on their cases, leading to a steep rise in detentions.

The agency, which falls under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), has also come under scrutiny for its use of vehicle stops and high-speed chases, with some incidents leading to injuries. Last week, an immigrant in Austin was shot in the back after fleeing federal agents who had stopped him as he made a DoorDash delivery.

Read More on U.S.

Newsweek reached out to DHS for comment via email Thursday afternoon.

ICE Barred From Immigration Court Arrests

On Thursday, a federal judge in New York ruled that ICE could not continue to detain people at immigration court anywhere in the country.

Judge P. Kevin Castel, an appointee of George W. Bush, ruled in New York Thursday that a Trump administration-era policy of arresting immigrants at their court hearings was "arbitrary and capricious."

"People should not be arrested for doing exactly what the legal system requires of them," Oscar Sarabia Roman, staff attorney with the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a press release. "They should be able to come to court, take part in their cases, and leave without fear."

In 2025, a policy enacted during President Joe Biden's term to prevent agents from making arrests at courthouses was revoked, leading to detentions at both criminal courts and immigration courts.

That change was quickly challenged by immigrant advocates, who argued that federal agents should not be allowed to wait outside hearings waiting to detain people.

In March, the Department of Justice said the administration had erroneously used the 2025 memo to justify immigration court arrests, with the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York writing that the DOJ deeply regretted the error.

Castel criticized the Trump administration Thursday, saying there were no records indicating ICE had changed its policy, with the 2025 guidance never mentioning a change in courthouse arrests.

"The most likely explanation for this silence is that the position expressed in 2026, i.e., that immigration courts were never within the scope of the 2025 Policies, was a recent invention and not the intent at the time of the issuance of the 2025 Policies," the judge wrote.

While he did not rule the policy itself unlawful, Castel ordered that the 2025 policies be pulled back, effectively putting the Biden-era protections back in place around immigration courts.

"Today’s ruling is an enormous win for every noncitizen seeking to safely attend their immigration court proceedings," Amy Belsher, director of Immigrants’ Rights Litigation at the New York Civil Liberties Union, said in a press release. "For too long, we watched masked, often armed, ICE officers ambush noncitizens in courthouse hallways, throw immigrants to the ground, and tear sobbing children from their parents. But with today’s order, the Court made clear: ICE’s cruel, unjustified policy of conducting mass immigration arrests in courthouses is unlawful and cannot stand."

Vehicle Stops Memo: What We Know

A policy memo seen by The Associated Press Thursday showed agents had been told Wednesday to stop high-speed chases and only engage in vehicle stops once they have completed specific training.

The memo, signed by ICE executive associate director Marcos D. Charles, includes steps meant to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE agents, as well as the drivers they are targeting, and others in the cars or nearby.

ICE field office directors were told they must ensure agents are using federal vehicles with lights and sirens that are activated, so that the public knows law enforcement is involved in a stop, and all officers must wear and use their body-worn cameras.

Five agency-specific training courses are also available for agents to complete, and only those who have completed at least one may carry out a vehicle stop, the memo said. Only those who have received certain training can continue using so-called "pinning," where an agent uses their vehicle to trap or stop a car.

The change, which ICE was said to have downplayed as a regular adjustment, comes after Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was shot by a federal agent following a traffic stop, which he later fled in Austin, Texas.

Garces Perez was charged earlier this week with allegedly assaulting, resisting, interfering, and impeding a federal officer. The complaint included stills from the body camera of one of the federal agents involved in the initial vehicle stop, but not from the agent who allegedly shot him after a high-speed chase.

ICE has received funding for agents to be equipped with body-worn cameras, but the technology's rollout has been relatively slow, with DHS saying the federal government shutdown earlier this year was to blame. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have urged the agency to quickly get the kit in place, for increased accountability and transparency.

text:
☀️ Good morning from The Legal File! Here is the rundown of today's top legal news:

🏛️Supreme Court to weigh Trump's mandatory immigration detention policy

The US Supreme Court agreed on October 1 to hear a dispute over a policy by the Trump administration that subjects millions of immigrants who entered the US illegally to mandatory detention during their deportation proceedings.

In this latest legal battle over Trump's hardline immigration agenda to reach the top US judicial body, the justices face an issue that has divided lower courts as numerous lawsuits by migrants and advocacy groups challenging the policy have played out. The policy is one of a number of measures his administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation.

The justices took up the administration's appeal of a ruling against the policy by the New York-based 2nd Circuit in a case involving a Brazilian national. SCOTUS will hear the case in its new term that begins on October 5.

The DHS in July 2025 issued new guidance to federal immigration officials announcing that immigrants in the US illegally are subject to mandatory detention without a bond hearing for the duration of their deportation proceedings, which can take months or even years to conclude.

The guidance represented a departure from a nearly three-decade-old interpretation of federal law that immigrants already living in the United States could be released on bond while they pursue their cases in immigration court.

The policy has produced an avalanche of lawsuits from immigrants seeking release. Immigrants have filed more than 73,000 such cases in federal court so far this year, about a quarter of all civil lawsuits brought in federal court.

Read more.

🤖California sets guardrails on lawyers' AI use

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed into law first-of-its-kind state legislation setting rules for how lawyers are permitted to use generative AI in their work.

Newsom signed the bill, SB 57 on September 30 alongside a slate of other AI-related measures that he said are intended to protect workers, empower doctors and prevent fraudsters online.

Courts across the country have imposed sanctions and issued warnings to lawyers who failed to vet AI-generated material and included “hallucinated” material in filings. Individual judges and courts have also issued standing orders setting guardrails on the use of AI.

No other state has enacted a law targeted at lawyers' and arbitrators' use of the technology, though some attorneys have said the measure is partly duplicative of existing rules.

“The legislation overlaps with existing legal ethics rules but serves as a reminder that lawyers need to be checking and verifying the output received from AI tools,” said Daren Orzechowski, a Silicon Valley-based M&A and technology transactions partner at A&O Shearman.

Under the new measure, an attorney cannot “delegate the practice of law” to generative AI. A lawyer responsible for submitting a filing in court must personally verify citations, including those provided by AI.

Read more.

⚖️New York attorney general named special prosecutor in Cornell rape probe

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she signed an executive order on October 1 appointing state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case of the alleged 2024 gang rape of a Cornell University student.

The student filed a civil lawsuit last month saying several members of a campus fraternity drugged and assaulted her in 2024. Hochul said that newly released information raised questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by Tompkins County prosecutors not to prosecute the case.

"I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it (the case)," Hochul said in a statement.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has acknowledged the public outcry about how authorities had handled the case. He said this week his office had reopened the case and would present evidence, including testimony from the woman, to a grand jury for possible indictment.

The case raised questions about how law enforcement and the university initially responded after the woman, then 20, made a report to police a few weeks after the alleged incident occurred.

Read more.

Related reads:

What we know about the Cornell University rape investigation

Alleged Cornell gang rape prompts calls to revise New York sexual assault laws

🗳️US Postal Service to take extra steps to ensure ballot deliveries

The US Postal Service said on October 1 it will take a series of extraordinary measures to ensure the delivery of millions of ballots for next month's 2026 congressional elections, including extending hours at some retail branches.

USPS said in a memo seen by Reuters that retail branches may extend hours starting Oct. 4 through the Nov. 3 election to handle ballots and establish a "Ballot Postmark Only" line at retail counters or a drive-through Ballot Mail option. USPS also will conduct expedited handling, extra deliveries, and special pickups of ballots..

USPS also said that before the election, workers can use the Priority Mail Express network to expedite the delivery of completed ballots returned by voters that might otherwise not be delivered in time. Starting October 24 through the election, carriers must check every delivery point for outgoing mail, regardless of whether they have incoming mail.

On September 14, SCOTUS declined to let USPS enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail.

The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.

Read more.

👋 That's all for today. Thank you for reading The Legal File, and have a lovely weekend!

authors: Rebecca Santana, Ali Swenson, immigration policy, ICE operations, employment-based immigration, apnews.com, rebecca-santana, ali-swenson
