text:
Key events

Family of Renee Good sues ICE agent who shot her and top Trump officials

Alba Asenjo Domínguez

The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, have filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration.

In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers.

Good was a US citizen and mother of three who, on 7 January, joined her wife in protesting against the deployment of thousands of ICE agents in their city as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation policy.

The 37-year-old was shot and killed in her car by an agent who claimed he acted in self-defense and the Department of Homeland Security claimed that she had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”. Multiple video clips of the encounter, however, show that Good was steering her vehicle away from the agent as she tried to drive away.

Her death and that of Alex Pretti, an American nurse who was also shot and killed by an immigration agent during Minneapolis protests two weeks later, sparked outrage and a wave of anger across the country.

Shortly after Good’s killing, Todd Blanche, then deputy attorney general, said he saw no grounds for opening a civil rights investigation. Days later, the justice department opened an investigation into the relationship between Becca Good, the deceased’s partner, and protest groups. At least 10 prosecutors resigned following the fatal shootings.

Now, these lawsuits have become some of the first major civil lawsuits filed against Trump’s deportation campaign in Minnesota.

In one of them, the attorneys for Good’s wife and brother allege wrongful death and seek damages for the “immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family”.

“The complaint also seeks to recover for Becca Good, who was standing feet from the couple’s vehicle when Ross fired three rounds into it, and she watched her partner die,” the complaint says.

“Peaceful assembly, speech and even dissent are protected rights. However, the government has distorted the exercise of these rights as violence against our republic and acted with extreme and unconstitutional force, causing egregious harm. Many of these illegal uses of force resulted in death – including the death of an American mother of three, Renee Good […] Today’s legal actions demand accountability for countless violations of the law, the Constitution and the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) own rules governing the use of force,” the lawsuit says.

The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials and federal immigration enforcement agents, and names Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot Good, the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, the White House deputy chief of staff and architect of hardline US immigration policies, Stephen Miller, and former US border patrol officer Gregory Bovino, among others, for their “roles in Renee Good’s death”.

Share

Trump refuses to commit to not demolishing Kennedy Center

Donald Trump also refused to rule out demolishing the Kennedy Center without the consent of Congress. Amid the ongoing high-stakes legal battle over the institution’s name and proposed renovations, the president told Time: “I’m not committing to anything. We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”

He added: “But if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I’m going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people … then I think the Trump administration should be recognized.”

A reminder that Trump has threatened to block proposed renovations to the Kennedy Center and suggested it could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it the “Trump-Kennedy Center” without congressional approval.

Per my colleague David Smith, Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way. Kerry Kennedy, JFK’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president.

“It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job.”

Trump also said earlier in the Time interview that he would be “willing to save it, but it’s in terrible, terrible shape.”

Attacking the judge who ordered his name to be removed from the facade of the building as a “radical-left Trump hater”, the president added:

double quotation markWell, why would I want to stick with something that’s going to lose hundreds of millions of dollars, and I’m not even recognized? It’s not me; it’s the administration.

The Trump-appointed board voted for the closure of the facility for two years earlier this month, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. But as David notes in his piece, Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and senator Sheldon Whitehouse have alleged that the proposed closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales following Trump’s takeover of the center when he returned to office.

Share

Updated at 12.59 EDT

The president remained convinced that Republicans chances of retaining control of Congress this midterm cycle remain strong.

“I think we’ll do OK if I campaign, and I intend to. If I campaign … you don’t give me enough credit. When I campaign, I give people a lot,” Trump told Time. “If I campaign for people, those people are going to win.”

At the GOP midterm convention last month, the president implored voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, in an effort to boost turnout. However, many Republican candidates running in battlegrounds where the president’s approval rating has cratered due to animus around Trump’s handling of the economy and ongoing war in Iran.

Share

Trump doesn't rule out sending ICE agents to polls in upcoming midterms

In his interview with Time magazine, Donald Trump did not rule out the possibility of sending federal immigration agents to polling sites in the upcoming midterms.

When asked, the president said: “Haven’t thought of it” and said that he “could” use the Insurrection Act to declare a national emergency. “A lot of people think I should use it sometimes,” he added.

However, it’s worth noting that legal experts say the law – which would allow the president to deploy troops domestically – doesn’t override the constitution, which prevents them from interfering with elections and appearing at polling sites.

Nonetheless, the administration has hinted at the idea of sending militarized federal agents to polls in recent months. In September, homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said that ICE officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country “to enforce specific threats”.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.”

Share

Supreme court says it will review whether Trump administration can detain immigrants while they challenge deportation

The supreme court today said it will review whether the Trump administration can enforce its policy of denying bond hearings for immigrants to determine whether they should remain detained while their cases are adjudicated.

The novel move to impose mandatory detention is another feature of Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown during his second term in office, and has now made its way to the top court after several appeals court judges ruled that the policy violated federal law and fails to provide immigrants with due process.

However, those decisions conflict with rulings by the fifth and eighth circuits – which ruled that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the US must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

The case that will be part of the supreme court’s docket for the 2026-27 term focuses on Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a citizen of Brazil, who authorities say he entered the US illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016 and was granted a work permit.

He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory after his September 2025 arrest. After Barbosa da Cunha sued, a federal judge ordered that be provided a hearing or released. An immigration judge found that Barbosa da Cunha did not present a flight risk or danger to persons or property, and ordered him released on bond. The administration appealed against the decision.

The number of people in immigration detention has shot up since Trump returned to office. It was more than 65,000 in July 2026, up from about 40,000 at the end of Joe Biden’s administration.

Share

Updated at 11.34 EDT

Donald Trump also claimed that “today” was the first he had heard of reports that Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, was warned prior to 7 October 2023 that there would be a likely attack by Hamas.

When Time pushed back, noting that Trump has “access to the highest intelligence”, the president dismissed concerns that Egypt and the United Arab Emirates altered Netanyahu in late September of that year that Hamas was planning a major operation.

“I can’t imagine this,” Trump said. “I don’t think so … I think if he would have known, he would have done something about it. Certainly, he would have had people at least alert.”

However, the president failed to give a clear answer on whether Netanyahu should serve for another term, ahead of Israel’s October elections.

Share

Updated at 10.53 EDT

Trump says that it’s ‘possible’ that strikes on Iran will increase after the midterms

Donald Trump defended the ongoing war with Iran, which appears to have little end in sight after the president rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Tehran, which he described in his Time interview as “not good enough”.

When asked whether he plans to ramp up bombings on Iran after the midterms, Trump said it was “possible”. The president also dismissed concerns from the Pentagon about munitions shortages as the war enters its seventh month.

“I would say it was mostly fake news,” Trump said. “Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms. We have that middle grade and upper middle grade, which is very powerful, which is stronger than it’s ever been before. There is ammunition that President [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy wouldn’t take, but it’s very powerful ammunition.”

Share

Capping off his tirade against the media during his interview with Time magazine, the president made sure to insult CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins, one of the many female reporters Trump has taken aim at during his second administration.

“I can name 100 great things I’ve done. I never get good press. I never get fair press. Doesn’t have to be good. All it has to be is fair,” he told Time. “So at a certain point, you say, ‘what’s the purpose of like this crazy Kaitlan Collins?’ She’s a very average person. She’s the most unhappy young person I’ve ever seen.”

Share

In that same interview, Trump insisted that he wasn’t defying the judge’s order by still preventing these outlets from covering the president at certain events.

“I don’t have to go out of my way, these people write only bad stories,” he said. The White House communications director, Steven Cheung, added that the judge’s order required the president to restore the newsrooms’ access to the White House, “but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One”.

If you recall, there is ongoing litigation about the Associated Press’ access to these so-called “intimate spaces” after Trump banned the outlet from them last year for refusing to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.

Share

Updated at 11.48 EDT

Trump continues to take aim at media in wide-ranging Time interview

Donald Trump doubled down on his attacks on the outlets he’s trying to ban from the White House in a wide-ranging Time magazine interview.

“I believe in an honest press, but I don’t believe in fake news,” he said, without providing any evidence about the areas of coverage he believes to be incorrect.

The president also said that Timothy Kelly, the federal judge who temporarily blocked the president’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now, was “very anti-Trump”. However, Trump actually appointed Kelly during his first term in office. When the Time interviewer reminded the president of this fact, he simply replied: “Yeah, he was. He was. It’s one of those things.”

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is laying out its policy on which officers can stop vehicles, and what is required to do when they're stopped, according to a memo obtained by ABC News and sources familiar with the change.

Formal guidance was issued to officers this week, sources said. This comes after several high-profile vehicle stops ended in shootings.

A Sept. 30 memo, which "amends" the agency's handbook for fugitive operations and "supersedes" previously issued guidance, states: "Effective immediately, only Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) offices who have successfully completed" certain of the agency's training courses "are permitted to conduct traditional vehicle stops, and call-back vehicle stops, commonly known as high-risk or felony vehicle stops."

Others who aren't properly trained can offer assistance, but cannot be the main officer in charge of the stop. In addition, only officers that have lights and sirens on their government-issued vehicles are allowed to stop cars, according to the sources.

The memo also states: "Under no circumstances are officers authorized to engage in vehicle pursuits or PIT maneuvers for vehicles that fail to pull over." Instead, officers are instructed to obtain vehicle information for further investigation.

An ICE spokesperson claimed the guidance is "nothing new."

"Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers," the spokesperson said in the statement. "This memo makes no changes to how ICE conducts vehicle stops. ALL officers have always received vehicle stop training."

The statement added: "Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue."

Earlier this summer, in the wake of two back-to-back fatal shootings -- one in Texas and one in Maine -- Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin temporarily paused traffic stops as ICE officers were set to receive new training.

However, President Donald Trump and others were reportedly furious about the pause, and Trump later overturned it, according to multiple sources at the time.

The new guidance doesn't prohibit vehicle stops, according to sources.

ABC News has reached out to DHS for comment on the new policy.

The new changes were first reported by CNN.

Last month, A Venezuelan migrant delivering for DoorDash was shot by an ICE officer in Austin, Texas.

Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez has been charged with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer.

The criminal complaint alleges that during a traffic stop, immigration officers asked Wilber Garces-Perez "to place his vehicle in park and step out--orders which he allegedly ignored."

The complaint alleges Garces-Perez led them on a high-speed chase before one of the officers "caught up to Garces-Perez, who allegedly attempted to strike the officer with his car, causing the officer to fire his pistol."

Attorneys for Garces-Perez said he still has a bullet lodged in his back.

text:
The UN Working Group of Experts on People from African Descent warned on Wednesday that individuals of African descent who are migrating face racism and discrimination throughout their journeys, attributing this mistreatment to discriminatory migration policies implemented worldwide.

The UN experts stated:

For Africans and people of African descent, freedom of movement continues to be shaped by racial hierarchies with deep historical roots. While some are welcomed as ‘expatriates’, others face unequal treatment driven by racialised perceptions, despite the equal entitlement of all migrants to human rights and dignity.

The Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent presented a report to the UN Human Rights Council revealing that migration policies and outcomes for people of African descent continue to be shaped by historical and contemporary forms of racialisation, such as the slave trade.

On this issue, the experts detailed that current migration governance does not comply with human rights standards and reflects embedded racist attitudes through border management, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital surveillance in migration management, and the adoption of discriminatory labour migration frameworks that foster precarity.

This has resulted in several abuses against African migrants, including gender-based violence, limited access to vital services, labour exploitation, racial profiling, and denial of access to regular status and documentation. Additionally, the UN experts highlighted that people of African descent are compelled to migrate due to economic reasons, unequal trade, and climate vulnerability, yet global protection frameworks do not recognise these factors as legitimate grounds for protection.

Furthermore, the group criticised what is described as the externalisation of migration control beyond the borders of Northern states through the implementation of migration partnerships or development assistance with African countries. It stressed that these arrangements expand surveillance rather than genuine mobility and are marked by unequal power relations, with African and other countries of origin and transit required to align with the security agendas of Northern countries.

Relatedly, the experts emphasised that migration governance should not rely on deportation and removal but rather prioritise rights-based policies, underlining the need to establish safe and regular pathways that support regularisation and humane governance in migration.

Consequently, the UN working group recommended measures to strengthen rights-based migration governance and protect the dignity of all migrants, particularly those of African descent. These measures include reforming labour migration frameworks to uphold dignity and rights, adopting rights-based migration frameworks that promote cooperation, and implementing practices that prevent racial profiling and xenophobia against African individuals in migration.

Multiple factors drive African individuals to migrate, including poverty, high unemployment rates, climate-related events, armed conflicts, and in search of better living conditions and safety. The UN has previously described Africa as a “continent on the move”, with high numbers of migrants recorded both within the region and in Europe. In July 2026, the President of South Africa called on African countries to strengthen cooperation and tighten immigration enforcement regimes, amid a surge of xenophobic violence against migrants.

text:
The Honourable Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, together with Denys Uliutin, Minister of Social Policy, Family, and Unity of Ukraine, and Eivind Vad Petersson, State Secretary for the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway, co-hosted Pathways to Peace: Second International Conference on Returning Ukrainian Children, Detained Civilians, and Prisoners of War in Toronto, Ontario, on September 28 and 29, 2026.

At the conference, Minister Anand announced a series of initiatives to strengthen Canada’s support to Ukraine in bringing people home and ensure that those who return can access rehabilitation and reintegration services:

Coordinated response to child militarization in temporarily occupied territories

Partner: Hala Systems

Funding: $3 million

Description: Canada is supporting a pioneering response to the evolving threats facing Ukrainian children, addressing not only deportation, but also indoctrination, militarization and recruitment. The project will strengthen cooperation between state and civil society partners by identifying children at risk, facilitating the safe return of children and providing immediate post-arrival support to children and their families.

Rescue and resilience for Ukrainian civil society

Partner: German Marshall Fund

Funding: $1 million

Description: Canada has previously announced the extension of a project with the German Marshall Fund to support local Ukrainian organizations in identifying and documenting cases, assisting families through complex return procedures, collecting evidence of human rights violations and coordinating with Ukrainian authorities and international partners. By strengthening these locally led efforts, the project assists in the safe return of children, supports families affected by separation and strengthens the capacity of Ukrainian civil society organizations to advocate and respond to the needs of affected children and their families.

Access to justice and healthcare assistance for male survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine

Partner: All Survivors Project Foundation

Funding: $500,000

Description: Canada is providing additional funding for an existing project to strengthen services for male survivors of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine, including prisoners of war and civilian detainees.

Canada Fund for Local Initiatives

Partner: Embassy of Canada to Ukraine, through the work of multiple local Ukrainian civil society organizations

Funding: $363,112

Description: Through the Canada Fund for Local Initiatives, the Embassy of Canada to Ukraine is supporting Ukrainian civil society organizations providing psychosocial, medical, legal, and reintegration assistance to formerly detained civilians and their families; legal support, advocacy, and trauma-informed services for families of POWs and missing persons; and education, skills development, and career guidance for youth returning from occupation, deportation, or displacement, helping them rebuild their lives and strengthen community resilience.

State reintegration services

Partner: UNICEF

Funding: $2 million

Description: This additional funding, announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney, supports UNICEF’s work with the Government of Ukraine to pilot its State Reintegration Service project in 15 communities. This state service will help establish a nationally defined pathway for returned children, connecting them and their families with the services they need for rehabilitation and reintegration.

Support to Ukrainian veterans and their families through a multi-donor pooled initiative

Funding: up to $40.1 million

Description: Canada and Ukraine are developing a multi-donor pooled initiative to support the implementation of Ukraine’s National Veteran Strategy, thereby providing support to Ukrainian veterans and their families. This initiative will further four broad areas of work: health, rehabilitation, and recovery; access to services and benefits; economic opportunity and livelihoods; and social inclusion and community participation for veterans and their families. Through this initiative, Canada will bring together governments, civil society organizations, and other stakeholders to foster coordination, share expertise and lessons learned as well as strengthen Ukraine’s long-term capacity to respond to the evolving needs of veterans. Canada and Ukraine are inviting interested partner countries to also contribute to this collective endeavour.

Sanctions on individuals involved in human rights violations of Ukrainian children

Description: On September 10, 2026, Canada announced new sanctions on eight individuals who have facilitated the Russian government’s violation of rights of Ukrainian children, including their unlawful deportation and forcible transfer, indoctrination and militarization. This brings Canada’s total number of sanctions on individuals who have facilitated Russia’s violations of Ukrainian children’s rights to over 120.

title: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids - NPR
description:
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life.
Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car.
At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke.
Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
text:
The family of Renee Good, the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.

One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.

It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.

The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.

It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."

In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.

"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges, including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."

Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.

According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.

"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."

Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.

In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."

The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.

The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges. DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.

At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."

At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.

"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."

Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.

In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.

"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."

title: The Supreme Court Just Took What Will Be the Blockbuster Case of the Term
description:
On Thursday, the U.S. Supreme Court accepted what is sure to be the blockbuster case of its 2026-2027 term.
The justices will consider head on if the Trump administration’s interpretation of two sections within the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act, Section 236 and 235(b), is lawful.
This interpretation has enabled ICE to round up undocumented immigrants en masse, with roughly 65,000 people in federal detention centers as of July 2026.
That is anyone’s guess, but the justices cannot come to that decision without also considering how the Trump administration’s interpretation of the INA has spun an astoundingly cruel immigration system.
The U.S. Supreme Court now has an opportunity to set the record straight on whether America should be a country welcoming to immigrants, or one that wants to rid itself of every single one.
text:
On Thursday, the U.S. Supreme Court accepted what is sure to be the blockbuster case of its 2026-2027 term. In Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the justices will consider the Trump administration’s novel interpretation of federal immigration law that has given it legal cover to systematically detain any undocumented citizen who entered the U.S. without permission, regardless of criminal history and without assessing whether they are a public safety threat or pose a flight risk. Hundreds of lower court judges, Democrat and Republican appointed ones, have been rejecting the Trump administration’s application of the law for the past year, and yet it’s enabled immigration agents to continue to detain tens of thousands of people in detention centers all over the country, a practice that has enabled some of the Trump administration’s most inhumane immigration policies.

The justices will consider head on if the Trump administration’s interpretation of two sections within the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act, Section 236 and 235(b), is lawful. The law gives federal authorities two options when faced with a deportation case of an undocumented person: Keep the noncitizen in federal custody while their immigration case goes through the courts, or release them on bond or parole. In recent history, all U.S. presidents choose to only apply the detention standard to recent border crossers, and any undocumented immigrants who have been living in the U.S. with established families and careers were eligible for bond or parole, so long as they were found not to be a public safety threat or flight risk. Last year, this standard drastically shifted, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, tasked with accomplishing the president’s mass deportation agenda, announced in July 2025 that the agency would begin detaining any and all undocumented immigrants facing removal orders, regardless of when they crossed the U.S. border, or if they had an established life here in the U.S.

This interpretation has enabled ICE to round up undocumented immigrants en masse, with roughly 65,000 people in federal detention centers as of July 2026. About 70 percent of these detainees have no criminal convictions. And as countless immigrants were rounded up, the courts were flooded with immigration cases, to the tune of over 20,000, prompting lower court judges to assess the Trump administration’s legal strategy and overwhelmingly reject it. U.S. District Court Judge of the Southern District of New York Lewis Kaplan wrote an especially damning decision when approving an undocumented immigrants’ habeas corpus petition last year: “The subject of immigration—including who lawfully can come into or remain in the United States, from where, for what reasons, in what numbers, and by what legal processes—is a subject committed by the Constitution to the Congress.” He went on to emphasize that the Supreme Court has also previously affirmed that immigration is a subject Congress has complete legislative power over and that the executive branch must only “‘take Care that the Laws’—enacted by Congress—be faithfully executed.’”

Kaplan continued by saying the Trump administration has every right to disagree with the way Congress wrote the INA, but the only way it can seek remedy is by going to Congress and asking to change the law, and muster up the necessary votes to pass new legislation. Recognizing the uphill battle that presents, the Trump administration chose not to go that route and instead applied a never-been-used-before interpretation of the INA in hopes of getting away with it for as long as possible, until the current Trump-friendly Supreme Court could weigh in.

It’s anyone’s guess how the justices will rule on this case, but it’s worth spending a minute considering how they’ve been ruling on immigration cases the Trump administration has routed its way over the past year. The court’s conservative majority has thus far allowed the president to end Temporary Protected Status for over 300,000 immigrants, turn away people seeking asylum at U.S.-Mexico land borders, and racially profile people targeted for immigration arrests. But the justices have also curbed the president’s deportation agenda with decisions that stopped unlawful deportations to El Salvador through the Alien Enemies Act and allowed the longstanding birthright citizenship clause of the Constitution to stand.

Will it allow the president to continue its mass detention policy? That is anyone’s guess, but the justices cannot come to that decision without also considering how the Trump administration’s interpretation of the INA has spun an astoundingly cruel immigration system. “Trump’s entire immigration arrest and detention policy regime *depends* upon its novel reading of the statutes,” Steve Vladeck, professor of law at Georgetown University and author of One First, noted on Bluesky.

Because ICE has been given the greenlight to arrest and detain every single undocumented immigrant with a removal order, Americans’ neighborhoods have been subjected to violent immigration raids that have pulled families apart and left U.S. citizens dead. It has also led to ICE agents stalking courthouses all over the country, immediately arresting people who were following the law and showing up to court-mandated hearings. And upon arrest, these immigrants have been thrown into decrepit detention centers where they’ve faced physical violence, sexual abuse, unsanitary conditions, and spoiled food. As of September 22, 2026, at least 27 people have died in ICE custody this year, while in 2025 there were 33 detainee deaths.

Making matters even worse, last month DHS began excluding immigrants detained with an outstanding removal order from the agency’s online detainee locator, making it nearly impossible for them to contact family or a lawyer.

It’s consistently been said that the cruelty here is the point, that the Trump administration wants to make life for immigrants so painful, they will simply leave on their own accord. The U.S. Supreme Court now has an opportunity to set the record straight on whether America should be a country welcoming to immigrants, or one that wants to rid itself of every single one.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Democracy Forward, a leading pro-democracy legal institution, today published The People’s Guide to the 2026-27 Supreme Court Term, the latest in its resources to help people better understand what is happening in the courts that affects their communities. The guide is a plain-language overview of key cases on the Supreme Court’s docket in the 2026-2027 term that highlights the impacts the cases will have on people. This guide is the third annual report on the Court from Democracy Forward and includes important information about the decisions this term that will shape the future of the rules governing elections, the rights of immigrants and LGBTQIA+ individuals, and the limits of government authority.

“An informed population is the backbone of democracy and Democracy Forward is committed to ensuring people have the tools they need to join the fight for their rights and an enduring democracy for all,” said Skye Perryman, President and CEO of Democracy Forward. “The People’s Guide to the Supreme Court is the latest in our series of tools that help make the judicial system and Supreme Court process understandable, so people can more effectively engage in the process and defend our democracy. We are grateful to have so many partners in this work, and hope this tool will be useful as the Court makes major decisions in the coming term.”

The “People’s Guide” includes background information and perspectives about cases on the Court’s “Merits Docket,” or cases that are scheduled and argued, in public, before the justices. The guide also tracks a series of cases on the Court’s “Shadow Docket,” or significant emergency petitions often decided with little to no transparency on extremely expedited timelines.

The cases featured in this year’s People’s Guide include:

Merits Docket

Suncor Energy U.S.A. Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County – Whether federal law prevents state and local governments from holding oil companies accountable for the negative effects of climate change.

Johnson v. United States Congress – Whether a federal law regarding veterans’ benefits can be challenged as unconstitutional in federal district court or only through specialized administrative and judicial review channels established by Congress.

Salazar v. Paramount Global – Whether a company’s disclosure of a website user’s Facebook ID and video viewing history to create targeted advertising violates the Video Privacy Protection Act.

St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy – Whether a Colorado law providing public funding to preschool programs that agree not to discriminate based on sexual orientation and gender identity violates the First Amendment rights of a religious school that objects to those terms.

Nielsen v. Watanabe – Whether an incarcerated man alleging inadequate medical treatment for a fractured tailbone can bring a constitutional claim for money damages against the prison officials he claims denied him that treatment.

Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards – Whether a federal agency can use its own administrative proceedings, rather than a federal court, to issue monetary fines to employers that violate the rights of seasonal farmworkers.

Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia – Whether employees at federally funded educational institutions can sue their employers under Title IX for sex discrimination in employment.

Wassily v. Blanche – Whether noncitizens who received and then lost asylum protections can still become Lawful Permanent Residents.

Viramontes v. Cook County – Whether laws banning semi-automatic rifles violate the Second Amendment.

International Partners for Ethical Care v. Ferguson – Whether parents can prospectively challenge state laws allowing transgender youth who run away from home to access gender-affirming medical care without parental notice or consent.

Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota – Whether Arizona can enforce voter suppression laws requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration and allowing county officials to purge registered voters immediately before Election Day.

Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D. – Whether and under what circumstances the Trump-Vance administration can deport immigrants in the United States to countries to which they have no connection, a practice known as “third-country removals,” without first providing them with notice and an opportunity to contest the third-country removal on the basis of having a fear of persecution, torture, or death in that country.

Shadow Docket (recent decisions on emergency petitions for immediate relief while litigation proceeds)

People Not Politicians v. Onder – Repeatedly rejecting Missouri’s attempt to use a congressional map favored by Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections.

National Republican Congressional Committee v. Brown – Allowing political parties to receive the same favorable broadcast advertising rates as individual candidates.

National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation – Allowing the Trump-Vance administration to continue using taxpayer funds to construct a ballroom following the unauthorized demolition of the East Wing of the White House.

United States Postal Service v. California – Halting the Trump-Vance administration from implementing last-minute restrictions to mail-in voting ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

M.W. v. Superior Court of California – Refusing to block a state court ruling granting legal parentage to a critically ill newborn’s intended parents rather than their gestational surrogate.

Department of Homeland Security v. League of Women Voters – Allowing the Trump-Vance administration to combine a federal immigration database known as SAVE with Social Security data to check the citizenship of people on state voter rolls, and for other purposes. What you need to know about that decision.

“For the past two years, our People’s Guide to the Supreme Court has tracked the intense speculation and uncertainty about how this Court would respond to a president determined to push the boundaries of executive power. Before President Trump returned to office, there was considerable debate over the willingness of the justices — including the three he appointed in his first term — to use judicial power to check his administration if necessary,” reads the guide’s introduction. “Now we have a clearer picture. The Court has largely ruled in favor of the administration, particularly in shadow-docket applications, with a handful of notable exceptions, including with respect to our elections. Justice Elena Kagan recently defended her colleagues by stating that the justices are ‘not a rubber stamp’ for the president. Whether that statement reflects genuine confidence in the Court’s independence, or something closer to wishful thinking, is worth watching. This term, we’ll be tracking not just how the Court rules, but how it uses procedural tools like the shadow docket to get there.”

text:
Over 30 organizations submit emergency UN request after ICE removes individuals with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System

September 30, 2026, Washington, DC – Earlier today, a group of over 30 organizations petitioned the United Nations Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (WGEID) to intervene after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) removed thousands of detained immigrants with final orders from its Online Detainee Locator System (ODLS) on September 15, limiting their access to legal counsel, the court system, and due process.

ODLS is an online system used to track the locations of individuals in ICE custody. Originally created in 2010, it has become an especially crucial tool for attorneys, families, and community members amid the Trump administration’s extraordinary efforts to arrest, detain, and deport noncitizens – often without notice or due process, and pursuant to third-country agreements.

Detained immigrants are regularly transferred among hundreds of detention sites nationwide. Without ODLS, family members have no way to locate their detained loved ones, and attorneys cannot pursue legal avenues of relief for their clients, including motions to reopen, appeals, habeas petitions, or stays of deportation.

“The new ODLS policy is aimed at forcibly disappearing and secretly detaining noncitizens with final orders of removal,” said the signatories. “By subjecting noncitizens to this policy, the United States has placed these individuals beyond the reach of legal protections, and rendered them particularly vulnerable to unlawful detention and deportation.”

ICE made no public announcement or warning prior to this new policy change, leaving attorneys and family members to scramble for information after their clients and loved ones’ locations were removed from the system on September 15.

In one case cited in the petition, attorneys at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center were unable to locate their clients – a breastfeeding mother and her 7-year-old daughter – after their abrupt removal from ODLS, temporarily obstructing the clients’ access to counsel and leaving family members terrified about their possible deportation. Other participating organizations highlighted similar client stories, including an LGBTQ+ asylum seeker from Ghana whose legal team at Human Rights First has been unable to pursue lawful avenues for relief because they cannot confirm his location.

One client quoted in the report described the terror he felt when his mother, an elderly asylum seeker with a disability, disappeared from the ICE locator: "We speak on the phone at least three times every day. Several days ago, I became extremely frightened when, because of a technical problem, phone service at the detention facility was suddenly cut off. She did not call me the entire day, and by that evening I checked the ICE detainee locator webpage and discovered that she had disappeared from it. I almost had a heart attack because she had always been listed there, and then she suddenly vanished. At that moment, the darkest thoughts imaginable went through my mind as to what my mother could be going through.”

The participating organizations called upon the UN WGEID to issue a formal declaration stating that the new ODLS policy is a form of enforced disappearance; recommend an immediate end to the policy; and conduct an urgent on-site trip to the United States to investigate.

"At the Center for Constitutional Rights, we have two clients who have been 'disappeared' from the ICE online locator," said Senior Staff Attorney CJ Sandley. "Thankfully we know where they are currently, but they could be whisked away in the dark of night to another detention or a third-country, and we would not know where they are for hours or days. This is, of course, a strategic move on ICE's part: to further isolate people from their communities and lawyers in moments of high need. We are asking the U.N. Working Group to call this what it is: unlawful disappearances."

The UN WGEID was created in 1980 to investigate enforced disappearances, which are formally defined as “the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the State” followed by “a refusal to acknowledge the deprivation of liberty or by concealment of the fate or whereabouts of the disappeared person.” The UN Human Rights Committee has previously determined that such disappearances violate the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which the United States ratified in the early 1990s.

The full list of signatories includes Abolitionist Law Center, Human Rights Program; Acacia Center for Justice; ACLU of Louisiana; American Gateways; Americans for Immigrant Justice; Amnesty International; CAIR-Chicago (The Chicago office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations); Cameroon Advocacy Network; Center for Constitutional Rights; Chicago United Families Coalition; Estrella del Paso; Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project; Haitian Bridge Alliance; Human Rights First; Immigrant Children Advocates' Relief Effort (ICARE); Immigrant Defenders Law Center (ImmDef); Immigrant Legal Resource Center; Law Offices of Stephen C. Zollman; Lawyers for Good Government; LSN Legal LLC; Mountain State Justice; New Jersey Consortium for Immigrant Children; Prisoners' Legal Services of New York; Public Counsel; RAICES; Refugees International; Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center; Sur Legal Collaborative; The Immigration Project Inc.; VECINA; Witness at the Border; and Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights

title: Judge issues final ruling against ICE immigration court arrest policy in Manhattan
description:
MANHATTAN (CN) — A federal judge granted summary judgment on Thursday to migrant rights groups who sued Immigration and Customs Enforcement over the agency’s controversial arrests at immigration courthouses.
U.S. District Judge P. Kevin Castel already blocked ICE from making these scrutinized arrests in New York City, barring limited circumstances.
Without that legal backing, Castel flipped his ruling in May and blocked ICE from continuing to make these arrests in three Manhattan immigration courts.
In another, a federal judge found ICE made an arrest within the guidelines for Castel’s stated exceptions, based in part on the arrestee’s criminal history.
Viral videos captured at Manhattan’s largest immigration court, 26 Federal Plaza, showed the sometimes violent practice in action.
text:
MANHATTAN (CN) — A federal judge granted summary judgment on Thursday to migrant rights groups who sued Immigration and Customs Enforcement over the agency’s controversial arrests at immigration courthouses.

U.S. District Judge P. Kevin Castel already blocked ICE from making these scrutinized arrests in New York City, barring limited circumstances. But in his new 36-page order, he finds the practice was wholly arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The government didn’t even try to argue otherwise, according to the George W. Bush appointee — he found its briefs “are silent as to whether the policy is arbitrary and capricious.”

Prior to the second Trump administration, ICE historically veered away from such detentions amid fears they could discourage dutiful court attendance. Castel initially greenlit the practice last September, siding with the agency that an agency memo from May 2025 justified them.

But earlier this year, ICE admitted in court that the memo didn’t actually justify these arrests at all. Federal prosecutors apologized to the judge for the “material mistaken statement of fact that the government made to the court” when previously arguing otherwise. Without that legal backing, Castel flipped his ruling in May and blocked ICE from continuing to make these arrests in three Manhattan immigration courts.

The judge found the agency now appears to have “no policy whatsoever” regarding these arrests and must continue to be precluded from making them.

“In this court’s view, ICE’s policy as to arrests in immigration courthouses is that officers may exercise ‘unfettered discretion … with no guidance whatsoever,’” he wrote.

Castel added: “The court rejects defendants’ argument that an arrest policy, or absence of an arrest policy, is beyond judicial review because the place of an arrest is left entirely to the discretion of the agency.”

Additionally, prior to ICE acknowledging the 2025 guidance never applied to immigration courts at all, the agency never provided “an acknowledgment of or reasoned explanation for the change in policy” in the first place, according to Castel.

“It is therefore arbitrary and capricious,” he wrote.

New York Civil Liberties Union lawyer Amy Belsher, who represented the plaintiffs, called the ruling “an enormous win for every noncitizen seeking to safely attend their immigration court proceedings.”

“For too long, we watched masked, often armed, ICE officers ambush noncitizens in courthouse hallways, throw immigrants to the ground, and tear sobbing children from their parents,” Belsher said in a statement. “But with today’s order, the Court made clear: ICE’s cruel, unjustified policy of conducting mass immigration arrests in courthouses is unlawful and cannot stand.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The underlying case was brought by immigration groups African Communities Together and The Door, which claimed in a lawsuit last August that the arrests are “unreasoned and contrary to law.”

“For decades, federal officials have avoided making civil arrests at courthouses for reasons recognized at common law and incorporated into the Immigration and Nationality Act: such arrests chill access to the courts and impede the fair administration of justice,” the groups argued.

Since Castel’s block on the practice, arrests at Manhattan immigration courts have slowed significantly, but they haven’t stopped completely, according to the government. In at least one case, the agency made an arrest and released the detainee within 24 hours. In another, a federal judge found ICE made an arrest within the guidelines for Castel’s stated exceptions, based in part on the arrestee’s criminal history.

The agency has also used anti-ICE protests as a way to justify making arrests at sensitive locations like immigration courts by arguing alternative areas would be “unsafe."

The practice has been a contentious centerpiece of President Donald Trump’s broader immigration enforcement agenda around the country. Viral videos captured at Manhattan’s largest immigration court, 26 Federal Plaza, showed the sometimes violent practice in action. In one instance, ICE agents shoved and injured a photojournalist while making an arrest in the building’s 12th-floor hallway.

text:
(NewsNation) — The family of Renee Good, the 37-year-old woman and mother of three fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Minneapolis in January, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government as well as federal immigration officers Thursday in Minneapolis.

Good’s death was the first of nine ICE-involved shootings this year. It sparked large-scale protests in Minneapolis that intensified after the shooting death of Alex Pretti by federal agents later in January.

The ICE officer who shot and killed Good, Jonathan Ross, was reassigned within ICE and transferred out of Minnesota after being placed on administrative leave.

Attorneys with Chicago-based law firm Romanucci and Blandin announced the filing of the two civil lawsuits at a news conference in Minneapolis. The firm, which commissioned an independent autopsy of Good’s body at the request of her family, is representing Good’s family along with Minneapolis attorney Kevin Riach.

The lawsuits are being brought by her brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good. Although the two were not legally married, Becca and Renee Good referred to each other as wives.

Ross is listed as a defendant in one of the lawsuits along with other federal agents who were at the scene of Good’s fatal shooting on Jan. 7. The lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights.

At the time, former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said Ross sustained internal bleeding and was hospitalized after he said he was hit by Good’s vehicle as Good attempted to leave after being instructed to by ICE officers.

The other lawsuit, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.

The independent autopsy, completed in January, showed Good was shot three times but the fatal shot was to her head. Good had two apparent gunshot wounds to her right chest, one on her left forearm and another possible wound on the left side of her head, the report said.

Good’s brothers testified on Capitol Hill in February. They spoke against what Democratic lawmakers referred to as the “violent tactics and disproportionate use of force” used by federal agents and officers during immigration enforcement operations in cities like Minneapolis and Chicago.

“This is not just a bad day or a bad week or isolated incidents,” Good’s brother, Luke Ganger, testified, calling the actions of federal officers “beyond explanation.”

He added, “These encounters with federal agents are changing communities and many lives — including ours forever.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

text:
Shortly before announcing his own retirement, a federal immigration judge in Chicago ruled on Tuesday that the Trump administration can deport Palestinian-American human rights activist Salah Sarsour under a controversial law that Secretary of State Marco Rubio has used to target activists who speak out against Israel’s genocide in Palestine.

Sarsour is an award-winning human rights activist and the president of the largest mosque in Wisconsin, where he is a beloved advocate and organizer. Along with anti-genocide activists such as Rumeysa Ozturk and Mahmoud Khalil, Sarsour was targeted for removal after he was singled out by Zionist groups in response to his advocacy for Palestine, making his case a major test of the First Amendment under President Donald Trump.

“While today’s decision is deeply disappointing, I will not give up,” Sarsour said in a statement on Wednesday.

After four hearings featuring testimony from multiple witnesses, the judge rejected allegations that Sarsour obtained his green card through fraud and falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen in order to vote. Sarsour had denied both charges.

However, under a Cold War-era law that has been weaponized by the Trump administration to target pro-Palestine activists and make a fascist spectacle of their arrests, the judge ruled Sarsour can be deported based on Secretary Rubio’s assertion that his advocacy for Palestinian liberation could have “adverse consequences” for U.S. foreign-policy interests.

The judge also deferred to Israeli charges against Sarsour dating to the late 1980s and early 1990s, when Sarsour was growing up in the West Bank. At a previous deportation hearing, Sarsour’s former attorney brought up his client’s experience in Israel’s military court system, sharing with the deportation court that Israeli intelligence officers tortured him so severely that they brought him to a hospital. He was ultimately convicted in that Israeli military court system, which convicts over 96 percent of Palestinians charged. Experts during Sarsour’s deportation hearings testified that Israel regularly arrests Palestinian youth on bogus charges based on false confessions extracted using torture.

“In my case, all evidence was thrown aside, and instead, a foreign country’s false information and unjust military courts were used to trample on my rights and ignore the truth,” Sarsour said. “But this fight is bigger than me, and I will not stop standing up for what’s right and for justice in Palestine.”

After being jailed and tortured by Israel as a teenager, Sarsour came to the United States in the 1990s as a lawful permanent resident. His family includes his six citizen children.

“A great deal of evidence that we presented was ignored,” said Patrick Taurel, one of Sarsour’s attorneys, during a press conference on Wednesday. “We know the records ICE filed were incomplete, and we know the government of Israel had no evidence — none — that Salah engaged in these activities for which he was convicted, besides false confessions signed in Hebrew.”

Sarsour is a board member of American Muslims for Palestine and was arrested by federal agents near his home in March after years of pro-Palestine advocacy. By fighting against his own deportation, Sarsour said he is defending a “vision of America where everyone can speak out against injustice without fear of government retaliation.”

The removal proceedings against pro-Palestine activists with green cards are the result of a partnership between far right and Zionist groups and senior members of the Trump administration that aims to crush pro-Palestine organizing and silence advocates for Palestinian liberation, according to the Center for Constitutional Rights.

Mahmoud Khalil, an activist who led anti-genocide protests at Columbia University, filed a lawsuit in July alongside the Center for Constitutional Rights against Canary Mission, the Heritage Foundation, Trump adviser Stephen Miller, and others. They allege that Project Esther has served as a blueprint for dismantling the pro-Palestine movement on college campuses, violating the Ku Klux Klan Act, which Congress passed in 1871 to address violent white supremacist paramilitaries during the southern Reconstruction.

Khalil has also sued Columbia University for failing to protect pro-Palestine student activists from harassment and political retaliation.

Project Esther and related campaigns attacked activists with baseless accusations of “terrorism” and “antisemitism” in order to make them targets for deportation. Like Sarsour, Khalil was also arrested at his home in March. Khalil spent 104 days in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, including at a prison in Louisiana that is more than 1,000 miles from his family in New York.

In September 2025, a federal court in Massachusetts found that targeting non-citizen students and faculty for arrest and deportation due to their political speech is unconstitutional. The landmark ruling by Judge William G. Young declared that non-citizens have the same free speech rights as citizens under the First Amendment.

However, in Sarsour’s case, Judge Jayme Salinardi ruled that Rubio’s letter identifying Sarsour’s advocacy as a threat to U.S. foreign policy is sufficient evidence for removal from the U.S. regardless of whether Rubio’s claims are factual, according to Taurel.

“You have to throw any notion that you have about due process out the window, the judge cannot act as a fact finder in this case,” Taurel said.

Salinardi was brought in from out of state to oversee Sarsour’s case and announced his retirement in court shortly after issuing the ruling. Immigration courts have suffered a wave of resignations and retirements by judges amid Trump’s mass deportation campaign, which has clogged the system and severely undermined due process.

Unlike the independent federal judiciary, immigration courts are separately run by the Department of Justice, where Salinardi and other judges are employees. They are ultimately under the Trump administration’s purview and can be fired; the administration has already purged more than 100 immigration judges.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has boasted about reducing immigration from majority Muslim countries by 96 percent and has stripped refugees of their legal protections — unless they are white people from South Africa.

“We know that there is a tremendous amount of pressure on immigration judges at this point in time, and we feared this outcome,” Taurel said. “But Salah is determined to continue speaking out. He has the soul of a lion, he will not be silenced, and he will not be cowed.”

The next step for Sarsour’s team is filing with the Board of Immigration Appeals, where they are expected to argue that Sarsour is likely to face persecution and torture if he is returned to Palestine under the Israeli occupation. Under federal laws that codify the UN Convention Against Torture, the government cannot deport people to countries where they are likely to face persecution.

If the Board of Immigration Appeals rejects Sarsour’s arguments, then his team will appeal to a federal district appeals court where, unlike Salinardi, the judges are independent from the Trump administration.

“We believe we will be vindicated on appeal when we get out of the immigration court system and get into an independent court,” Taurel said. “He is going to be here for the foreseeable future.”

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is changing its policy on which officers can stop vehicles, and what is required to do when they're stopped, according to sources familiar with the change.

Formal guidance was issued to officers this week, sources said. This comes after several high-profile vehicle stops ended in shootings.

Only those ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officers who have completed the relevant training may participate in the stops, according to the sources, who said others who aren't properly trained could only offer assistance, but not be the main officer in charge of the stop.

In addition, only officers that have lights and sirens on their government-issued vehicles are allowed to stop cars, according to the sources.

Earlier this summer, in the wake of two back-to-back fatal shootings -- one in Texas and one in Maine -- Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin temporarily paused traffic stops as ICE officers were set to receive new training.

However, President Donald Trump and others were reportedly furious about the pause, and Trump later overturned it, according to multiple sources at the time.

The new guidance doesn't prohibit vehicle stops, according to sources.

ABC News has reached out to DHS for comment on the new policy.

The new changes were first reported by CNN.

Last month, A Venezuelan migrant delivering for DoorDash was shot by an ICE officer in Austin, Texas.

Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez has been charged with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer.

The criminal complaint alleges that during a traffic stop, immigration officers asked Wilber Garces-Perez "to place his vehicle in park and step out--orders which he allegedly ignored."

The complaint alleges Garces-Perez led them on a high-speed chase before one of the officers "caught up to Garces-Perez, who allegedly attempted to strike the officer with his car, causing the officer to fire his pistol."

text:
Before federal immigration agents stormed across the Chicago region last year and President Donald Trump threatened to send in the National Guard, Gov. JB Pritzker warned both moves aimed to “normalize” a federal military presence to intimidate voters and depress turnout in the 2026 midterms.

Some at the time viewed Pritzker’s contention as a bit of a stretch, given federal laws prohibit armed civil or military personnel at the polls and state laws bar election interference. But as the immigration surge grew chaotic, combative and deadly in Chicago through Operation Midway Blitz and in other operations throughout the country, the governor’s concerns gained traction.

Now, citing recent comments by Trump and top administration officials, voting rights activists and Democratic officials have filed at least two lawsuits in federal court in Washington that seek to block what they contend is a “polling place policy” that would allow U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and FBI agents to operate in or around polling places.

At the same time, local county clerks and election officials in Illinois have stepped up planning for various scenarios involving federal activity at the polls. Their options include deploying lawyers to federal and state court to seek injunctions and using local law enforcement to make arrests under state law.

“A polling place should be a safe and protected civic space where every eligible voter can walk through the door, cast their ballot and leave without fear or intimidation,” Cook County Clerk Monica Gordon said last week after a roundtable of local officials and voting rights advocates in west suburban Franklin Park. “The polling place belongs to the voters on Election Day. Our job is to make sure they can exercise their right to vote safely, securely and without interference.”

The general election is Nov. 3, less than five weeks away, and early voting in Chicago starts Thursday at the Early Voting Super Site, 137 S. State St., and the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners’ offices at 69 W. Washington St., on the 6th floor.

Over the past three months, staff from Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office and the Illinois State Board of Elections staff have held weekly virtual meetings with local election authorities around the state. The meetings initially focused on federal court rulings that rejected Trump-led efforts to restrict mail-in balloting. But they have “fed into other conversations” about the potential for federal intervention in the election, said Lake County Clerk Anthony Vega.

“This is a heightened resource, or at least a mechanism, for having those higher-level conversations and they’re super helpful,” Vega said, because “elections are run at the local level (and) it’s going to be up to the clerks to really be the driver in terms of preparation.”

“Since we run elections at the very local level, sometimes it can be very isolating. Being able to get together is very beneficial,” said Vega, who also has been hosting webinars with Lake County State’s Attorney Eric Rinehart on election interference issues, including one set for Oct. 14.

Voters share election officials’ concerns. A Suffolk University/Chicago Tribune survey of 500 adult Chicago residents conducted in April found 64% said they were concerned immigration agents would reemerge around the general election, while 31% said they don’t share that concern. The poll’s margin of error was 4.4 percentage points.

“We know that a number of constituents continue to make calls, whether it’s directly to their member of Congress, whether it’s the Board of Elections or a state senator or a city council person or (speak) among family members at the dining room table: ‘Will we be able to vote this year?’ ‘Will it be safe to go out and vote?’ ‘Will my vote count … and when I go to vote, will I be threatened? Will I be in any way harassed or in any way feel the fear to go vote because perhaps there is a deployment of ICE agents there?'” U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez said after the Franklin Park event.

“The president has weaponized fear and division and abused every authority and power to erode social trust and undermine democratic institutions,” the Democratic congresswoman said.

A federal court case filed in September on behalf of Hispanic civil rights groups, voting rights group Common Cause and the city of Denver, Colorado, as well as a lawsuit filed by various campaign entities of the Democratic National Committee and congressional Democratic leaders, cite a number of statements from Trump and the administration that they say warrant judicial action.

In May, when reporters asked Trump about sending the National Guard or ICE agents to polling locations, he said he would “do anything necessary” to hold what he viewed as an “honest election.”

On Sept. 1, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the administration’s policy could include sending immigration agents to polling places to conduct enforcement operations, including serving warrants and detaining people suspected of being unlawfully present in the country.

Two weeks later, FBI Director Kash Patel was asked during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing if he planned to send agents to the polls. He replied, “Election integrity is of paramount importance.” Asked whether he would pledge not to interfere with the will of voters going to the polls Nov. 3, Patel responded, “I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies.”

“Notwithstanding federal law, and the traditional sanctity afforded to polling places, the Trump administration has made clear by word and deed over the past year that it asserts the authority to dispatch armed officers to active polling locations,” the Democrats’ lawsuit contends.

A federal statute enacted by Congress just weeks before President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in 1865 prohibits “armed men” in the “civil, military or naval service of the United States” from being present “where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Additionally, federal law prohibits any person “whether acting under color of law or otherwise” from intimidating, threatening or coercing any other person “for voting or attempting to vote,” or “urging or aiding” someone else to vote or attempt to vote.

The Illinois Constitution prohibits denying the right to vote “based on race, color, ethnicity, status as a member of a language minority, national origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation or income.” In addition, anyone who “by force, intimidation, threat, deception or forgery knowingly prevents any other person” from lawfully voting “is guilty of a felony.”

It also gives election judges the power to seek the arrest of anyone for the “breach of the peace or for any breach of election laws” or interference with the election and requires law enforcement to follow such an order “as if a warrant had been issued.”

As has traditionally been the case, the Illinois attorney general’s office is sending out teams of assistant attorneys general and investigators to monitor the elections.

But the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners has gone a step further by retaining an outside law firm so it can go to court quickly if necessary.

Marisel Hernandez, who chairs the Chicago election board, said the election authority realized a year ago, with the launch of Operation Midway Blitz, that city polling places could face federal intervention in 2026.

“We started meeting with a number of law enforcement agencies — and that includes the FBI, the Chicago Police Department, the Illinois attorney general’s office, the Cook County state’s attorney’s office, the Illinois Board of Elections and the Cook County sheriff’s office as well — because we wanted to be prepared in case anything occurred and we wanted everybody to be on the same page with regards to a plan of action,” Hernandez said.

“We’re trying to do everything we possibly can to stay ahead of any potential issues and react accordingly,” she said.

At least one field investigator, usually a retired law enforcement officer, will be stationed at each early voting site, Hernandez said. On Election Day, 212 more field investigators and 50 ward supervisors will be on patrol, with 200 auxiliary field investigators on standby, she said.

“We’re determined to reassure the voters that everything proceeds as normal,” she said.

authors: Ryan J. Foley, “Lethal Restraint.” twitter mailto, apnews.com, ryan-j-foley
description:

After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops.
“Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.” The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
