But in areas like this one in Maine, organizers mobilizing against ICE’s deportation machine are often spread out and strapped for resources.
Organizers’ ICE-watching hotline received 128 calls the week that Durán was killed, according to MIRC’s Chitam.
The crew of ICE-watching volunteers helped her figure out how to get home.
Still, the organizers, volunteers and advocates making up Maine’s resistance to ICE will keep doing the work.
text:
Most of the time, the scene outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in the small, coastal town of Scarborough, Maine, could be confused for a nature watch in “Vacationland”, the slogan on state license plates.

People sitting in lawn chairs under a tent. Birds chirping. The sound of the breeze moving through the trees.

But when four Escalades zoom into the ICE facility parking lot on an August afternoon, the group springs out of their chairs, binoculars and clipboards in hand. Some rapidly call out license plate numbers, makes and models, while another scribbles the information down. This is what monitoring ICE operations looks like in the east coast’s most sparsely populated state: documenting the agency’s unmarked vehicles and keeping a record of detainments – the people arriving for routine appointments or brought in by agents and never seen leaving.

ICE-watching – following, documenting and alerting neighbors to federal immigration agents’ public activities – is a longtime, constitutionally protected practice that became more popular in response to the Trump administration’s ramping up of violent, on-the-ground immigration-enforcement operations last year. It particularly drew attention in Minneapolis in January, when neighbors came out in droves to record and interfere as agents pulled people out of cars, off sidewalks and from bus stops. Though ICE has shifted to less visible tactics since the start of the year, the number of immigration arrests is higher than ever, including in rural and suburban areas, such as much of Maine. ICE observers are still there, too – albeit exhausted and burned out.

In many of the US’s largest cities, immigrant rights networks count hundreds if not thousands of volunteers, and dozens of neighborhood-based encrypted chats and organizations activate on short notice.

But in areas like this one in Maine, organizers mobilizing against ICE’s deportation machine are often spread out and strapped for resources. The Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition (MIRC), a small non-profit representing more than 100 state-based organizations, estimates it has about 100 trained, regular volunteers on its roster. Some days, ICE-watching in the state is just three people in lawn chairs scrawling license plate numbers in their notebooks.

“People are trying the best they can – learning and utilizing new skills, and responding to crises in community – and then there’s another one, and there’s another one, and there’s another one,” said Crystal Cron, co-founder and executive director of Presente! Maine, a Latino-led organization that has given out about $200,000 in bond money for immigrants in detention every month since Donald Trump retook office through its solidarity fund.

But the work is never-ending, she said: “That is what the escalating violence is meant to do – it’s meant to exhaust us and confuse us.”

Recovering from an ICE surge

ICE-watching efforts in Maine ramped up in January, when the Trump administration launched Operation Catch of the Day, an intense crackdown on undocumented residents named in reference to the state’s $600m fishing industry that’s powered in part by migrant labor. In a state with a population a third of the size of the city of Los Angeles and where immigrants make up roughly 4% of residents, 100 people were arrested in three days, the majority of whom had no criminal records and were lawfully in the US.

Masked agents smashed car windows to abduct drivers, then abandoned the vehicles – and at least once, with a mother and baby inside – on the side of the road; children watched agents detain their parents from their front steps.

It “shocked the whole system”, said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the MIRC. “The tactic was much faster than the traditional system that we had envisioned. By the time somebody can call [in a sighting], somebody’s already been picked up.’”

Residents and local community groups in the state came together, following ICE vehicles and dropping off groceries for immigrant neighbors too scared to leave their homes.

The operation lasted for nine days, and soon after, public backlash over ICE violence across the US reached new heights. The killing of two ICE observers in Minneapolis sparked widespread protests and intensified scrutiny of the administration. Trump replaced Department of Homeland Security (DHS) leadership, directing ICE to adopt “a little bit of a softer touch”. But while agents have become less visible in public, in Maine they never went away.

In July, an ICE agent killed 25-year-old father Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a traffic stop in Biddeford, 15 minutes from Scarborough. This happened just days after an agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas, also during a traffic stop. Any illusion of ICE’s “softer touch” was shattered.

Organizers’ ICE-watching hotline received 128 calls the week that Durán was killed, according to MIRC’s Chitam. People in Biddeford once again took to the streets and elected officials demanded an investigation.

This time, though, already-traumatized and outraged residents felt pushed to the brink, organizers said. Many of the state’s immigrants have been effectively sheltering in place for the last nine months.

“The death of Johan has been devastating, but for us it was not a surprise,” said Cron. “Our communities have always been under threat of persecution. Being hunted in the streets is not new.”

Organizers had been preparing for this moment. Last October, the MIRC and other community groups such as the People’s Coalition for Safety and Justice launched their hotline to report ICE sightings. The MIRC also built a network of volunteers who could speak the many languages reflected in Maine’s immigrant population – Somali, Haitian Creole, Arabic – coordinated via the encrypted app Signal.

Since then, the MIRC’s handful of staffers have been triaging between state offices, other policy organizations and community members – from assisting business owners protecting immigrant employees to lobbying elected officials on what resources they need. In May, the MIRC and Presente! created Lighthouse ME, an online “immigrant defense hub” that includes ICE arrest data and a visual tracker of sightings.

To hold ICE accountable, the Maine chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union recently launched a hotline to report first amendment violations. During the operation ICE agents followed observers home to intimidate them, fired pepper balls at their cars and told residents they would be added to a “domestic terrorist” list. Those residents and other observers have since launched a federal class action lawsuit against the DHS.

“The constitution guarantees your right to observe and record law enforcement agents when they’re doing their job in public. And yet the government keeps finding new ways to try to interfere with people’s first amendment rights,” said Zach Heiden, chief counsel at the ACLU of Maine. “But if bringing a lawsuit is necessary, then that’s what we’re going to do, for as long as it takes.”

‘Anytime they’re here, we’re here’

While organizers in Maine and many other parts of the country have been stretched thin, ICE-watching remains robust in bigger cities, although the tactics are evolving.

In Chicago, a year after Operation Midway Blitz, ICE observers are still pounding the pavement, looking for agents and carrying whistles to alert their neighbors. But community support is now more focused on managing the trauma already suffered through planning cultural events and vigils.

While New York never saw the sweeping on-the-ground operations that Chicago, Maine or Minnesota did, the city’s large population is a boon for its ICE-watching network. A patchwork of non-profit organizations, longtime community organizing groups and mutual aid networks all support immigrant communities. Organizers with Hands Off NYC, which launched a year ago to organize against ICE, said there are at least hundreds of people who have taken know-your-rights training, offered online, in the last several months.

And yet despite Maine’s smaller ICE-fighting network, residents have already seen its impact on the state level: thirteen days after Durán’s killing, three “ICE Out” laws went into effect, blocking cooperation between the agency and local police forces, landlords, schools and state healthcare facilities.

Heiden, of the ACLU of Maine, observed that none of those laws would’ve saved Durán’s life, though. Many organizers said that much more needs to change to prevent another ICE killing. This weekend, residents plan to march 70 miles (113km) from the office of the senator Susan Collins in Biddeford to the state capital in protest of her support for ICE funding.

“Johan’s death is not an isolated tragedy. It is part of a system that has inflicted fear, separation, detention and death on immigrant communities,” Cron testified during a hearing in August. “The responsibility for his death, and the many deaths by immigration police and in ICE detention this year, is a collective one.”

And so residents continue to push for justice, accountability and structural change.

At a congressional “shadow hearing” in August – an unofficial proceeding hosted by the US representative Chellie Pingree investigating Durán’s killing – the Biddeford high school auditorium was packed with irate residents holding signs declaring “ICE = Terrorists, Democrat Silence = Complicity”.

When Durán’s parents walked in, a heavy hush fell over the room. Durán’s father, his voice thick with held-back tears, testified through an interpreter: “Our dream was always to be reunited and to hold each other again. Today that dream can no longer come true.”

On the same day, just 10 minutes away, another group of Mainers grieved and organized at Biddeford’s Mechanics Park. The site where French and Irish immigrants blocked the Ku Klux Klan from a planned march into Biddeford more than 100 years ago is now occupied by activists and an art installation – hundreds of ribbons tied to a fence with messages for Durán and the city’s immigrant residents. Nearby are stocks of snacks, Narcan, “know your rights” zines and 3D-printed whistles.

When a neighborhood kid drops by a tent and takes a free Gatorade from the cooler, he tells the person making “Fuck ICE” bracelets he’ll come back later. “We’ll be here,” she replies.

Meanwhile, at the Scarborough facility, observers say they’ve been seeing, on average, two detentions a day: people brought to the facility in shackles by ICE agents and people who arrive for appointments and never come back out, abandoning their cars. (Their estimate is borne out in DHS data monitored by the Guardian.) In their informal capacity, they have, at times, become the first line of support to dazed family members exiting the facility.

Still fresh in their minds is Jonas Manywa, a 42-year-old asylum seeker from the Democratic Republic of Congo who arrived at the facility for a routine appointment in early August. Agents arrested him in front of his two young daughters. When his wife came with their nine-month-old to pick up their children, she had his car keys but couldn’t drive. The crew of ICE-watching volunteers helped her figure out how to get home.

Most days, people stop by the tent at the Scarborough facility, dropping off water bottles and snacks for the volunteers and thanking them for their efforts. But even with this community support, it’s been difficult to recruit new volunteers.

“Now more than ever, we need people to join us to build a better, more free world,” said Cron.

Still, the organizers, volunteers and advocates making up Maine’s resistance to ICE will keep doing the work.

“Anytime they’re here,” one ICE observer said, looking at the Scarborough facility, “we’re here.”

title: 3 Californians amend immigration lawsuits after 'No Kings Act' signed into law | KTVU FOX 2
description:
Gavin Newsom this week signed the "No Kings Act" into law, allowing people to file lawsuits against ICE and other federal agents.
Javier Ramirez of East Los Angeles is one of the plaintiffs and he described his encounter with federal agents.
"No Kings Act" details The backstory: State Senator Scott Wiener of San Francisco authored the "No Kings Act" in 2025 following the Trump administration's aggressive federal immigration actions and takeover of Los Angeles.
And it was right after everything that played out in Los Angeles—just the attack by ICE on the people in Los Angeles.
If you want to regulate federal agents, you have to win a federal election.
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom this week signed the "No Kings Act" into law, allowing people to file lawsuits against ICE and other federal agents.

Immediately, an attorney in Los Angeles amended her lawsuits against the Department of Homeland Security and multiple John Doe federal agents, using the new law SB 747, for allegedly using excessive force and violating the constitutional rights of three U.S. citizens in 2025.

Civil lawsuits against ICE and other federal employees.

What they're saying:

"These people aren't criminals. They weren't doing anything wrong. They were going to work, they were just doing their jobs. These people are just ordinary people. They are American citizens. They were born here, and they're still being targeted," the plaintiff's attorney, Maria Garcia Baldizzone, said. She also provided video of the arrests.

Garcia Baldizzone is the attorney for the three plaintiffs in Southern California who say federal agents violated their rights.

Her amended lawsuits reference Wiener’s new law, which allows Californians to file civil lawsuits against any federal agent for violations of their constitutional rights, including not having probable cause.

Javier Ramirez of East Los Angeles is one of the plaintiffs and he described his encounter with federal agents. Ramirez is a U.S. citizen, but said he was grabbed by the agents on his property. They then threw him to the ground, video shows.

"One of them points me out and says, 'Aw, just get him, he's Mexican,'" Ramirez recounted in an interview on Wednesday. "I said, 'What are you doing? I'm a U.S. citizen."

He said he was arrested but never given access to an attorney or medical care.

"I never knew why I was detained, why I was arrested. They said I was detained for resisting arrest, impeding a federal investigation," Ramirez said.

A second case involves a U.S. citizen, Cary Lopez, who was nine months pregnant and says she was thrown against a vehicle by immigration officers.

"They did push her up against a car, kind of threw her against the car, and didn't pay attention to the fact that she was close to her due date," Garcia Baldizzone said.

She says she was detained and later released but blames the trauma on her giving birth to her baby prematurely.

A third plaintiff says he began videotaping immigration officers who were talking with some youth and says he was arrested.

"He ended up in the hospital. They hurt his arm, his shoulder, his back," Garcia Baldizzone said.

"No Kings Act" details

The backstory:

State Senator Scott Wiener of San Francisco authored the "No Kings Act" in 2025 following the Trump administration's aggressive federal immigration actions and takeover of Los Angeles.

He said the law closes a legal loophole that made it difficult to successfully take federal agents to court after the U.S. Supreme Court weakened efforts people could take when suing federal officers, which he said created "de facto immunity" from prosecution for officers who violate residents’ civil rights.

"I introduced this bill a year ago," Wiener said in an interview. "It was the first bill of its kind in the country. And it was right after everything that played out in Los Angeles—just the attack by ICE on the people in Los Angeles. We think we have a strong legal basis to say if a federal agent or border patrol violates your rights under the Constitution, you can sue them and get damages."

Critics say the new law is unnecessary.

On Wednesday, U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who works for the Central California District, posted a message online saying: "Governor, we've been through this already. If you want to regulate federal agents, you have to win a federal election. Until then, you have no jurisdiction."

The Department of Homeland Security also didn't respond for comment.

The law is retroactive to March 1, 2025, in order to include anyone who was impacted by federal agents in that city.

title: Polish Activists at Belarus Border Prosecuted for Aiding Migrants - Just Security
authors: Brian Dooley, Suchita Uppal, Eric Lee, Michael Mattler, Carol Rosenberg, Michael P. Scharf, Wells Dixon
description:
Those arriving at the Polish border often have been met with hostility and violence from Polish border guards and other security forces.
Yet, Poland is among the EU countries where people are most often prosecuted for helping migrants.
Legal Harassment Our organization, Human Rights First, has visited the border regularly since 2021, documenting attacks on activists and observing their trials.
Prosecutors accuse her of organizing illegal crossings of the Polish border by helping arrange routes and transportation.
Grupa Granica, an association of activists and NGOs providing aid at the border, and its members also routinely receive threatening comments on social media.
text:
Human rights defenders providing humanitarian, medical, and legal support to migrants and asylum seekers at Poland’s border with Belarus say Polish authorities continue to target them with prosecutions, interrogation, and home searches, even as the number of people trying to cross declines. Fading public attention and shrinking funding are leaving them vulnerable to government harassment as well as continuing online threats.

Since 2021, Belarus has encouraged and enabled tens of thousands of people to cross its border into Poland, apparently seeking to create political problems for the European Union amid lingering public hostility towards migrants and asylum seekers following the continent-wide crisis that peaked in 2015 and 2016, when millions arrived in Europe. As during that period, many people attempting to cross from Belarus into Poland — and increasingly into the Baltic countries of Lithuania and Latvia — are fleeing conflict and persecution in the Middle East and Africa. Those arriving at the Polish border often have been met with hostility and violence from Polish border guards and other security forces.

The Poland-based non-governmental organization (NGO) We Are Monitoring has recorded more than 13,000 pushbacks (forcing people seeking asylum back across the border) and at least 107 deaths at the border in the five years since the crisis began. Polish courts in several cases have found those pushbacks unlawful, and in July 2025 a court awarded compensation for the first time to two Afghan nationals detained without justification in 2021 and returned to Belarus.

Yet, Poland is among the EU countries where people are most often prosecuted for helping migrants. Brussels-based NGO Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants (PICUM) recorded at least 20 people facing legal proceedings in Poland in 2025, second only to Greece, which became notorious for tactics such as using equipment intended for sea rescues to instead push migrants’ vessels back into international waters. Even in recent days, EU and British foreign ministers met to discuss tightening border restrictions further.

Poland responded to the arrivals from Belarus by building a 5.5-meter-tall (about 18-foot-tall) steel fence, expanding electronic surveillance, creating a buffer zone, stationing soldiers at the border, and suspending the right to seek asylum there. The suspension, introduced in March 2025 for 60 days, has been renewed continuously since. On Sept. 18, Parliament approved the ninth consecutive extension by 418 votes to 16. Although it formally applies only at the border, activists say people who crossed there are blocked from seeking asylum even after traveling farther into Poland, as we outlined in a recent report. The law allows for exceptions for vulnerable groups, including pregnant women, but it is applied inconsistently and border guards decide who qualifies.

Crossings from Belarus have dropped sharply in the wake of these and other shifts. The Polish Interior Ministry recorded about 235 attempted crossings in the first half of 2026, compared with more than 15,500 during the same period last year. Yet, the pressure on those helping migrants has continued.

Legal Harassment

Our organization, Human Rights First, has visited the border regularly since 2021, documenting attacks on activists and observing their trials. We returned in August to meet activists and humanitarian workers in the region and published the above-mentioned report on the continued targeting and legal harassment they face.

The most prominent recent case of prosecution involved five activists who gave food, water, and clothing to a desperate Iraqi couple, their seven children and an elderly Egyptian man. Four of the activists also gave the group a ride to the nearest town, when they were stopped by border guards. Prosecutors charged the five activists, who’ve become known as the Hajnówka Five, under Article 264a § 1 of Poland’s Penal Code with facilitating unlawful stay for personal or material benefit. On Sept. 8, 2025, the District Court acquitted all five. Judge Adam Rodakowski determined that the provision required some gain to accrue to the accused and the activists had gained nothing.

Polish courts have reached similar conclusions in other cases. In May 2023, for example, the same court found that an Iraqi man who had travelled from Germany to help freezing relatives in October 2021 had not acted unlawfully. A study by the Szpila Collective and the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, both Polish NGOs, found that cases brought against activists in 2021 and 2022 were overwhelmingly discontinued or ended in acquittal. In September 2025, a volunteer known as Bartek, charged with influencing the official duties of the Polish Border Guard service after demanding access to a Somali client who was pushed back without his claim being registered, was acquitted, too. Yet an acquittal does not repair the damage. Investigations can remain open for years, consuming time and money while serving to intimidate anyone watching what may happen if they help.

Several serious cases remain open. Kamila M., one of the Hajnówka Five, was named a suspect in a separate investigation while her first trial was still underway. Prosecutors accuse her of organizing illegal crossings of the Polish border by helping arrange routes and transportation. Karolina M., a humanitarian worker, was charged by Polish prosecutors with organizing the movement of at least 15 people from Poland into Germany. She denies the charge and says she was providing humanitarian assistance. Activists familiar with the case say officers searched her home, seized electronic devices, and questioned her for about nine hours. Ewa M., a humanitarian worker arrested in 2023 and initially held in pretrial detention, is accused of leading a criminal group that organized unlawful crossings, an offense carrying up to 10 years in prison.

Portraying All Assistance as Suspicious

“When humanitarian cases are mixed together with smuggling cases, it becomes easier to portray all assistance as suspicious,” Aleksandra Chrzanowska of the Warsaw-based Association for Legal Intervention told us. Her organization provides legal and integration assistance to migrants and refugees. Ola Ziemiańska of Szpila, a Polish collective providing legal and psychological support to activists, described three patterns of repression: first, pressure through fines and misdemeanor proceedings, then high-profile prosecutions meant to intimidate a movement, and now the targeting of people seen as central organizers. Investigations can lie dormant for years and be revived when it is most politically beneficial, she said. She expects Karolina M.’s case to resurface during the 2027 national election campaign. The pressure does not come only from the courtroom. Mateusz Rybak was 14 when he began helping people stranded in the border forests. Now 18, he continues to volunteer there. As a result, he has been the target of death threats and abusive messages. Schoolmates once threatened to break his legs so he could no longer go to the forest. He faces online abuse regularly, and more recently, someone created and circulated pornographic deepfakes depicting him, and he plans to take legal action. He uses his social media following as a form of protection. “If people know who I am and are watching what happens to me, it’s harder to target me quietly,” he said. Grupa Granica, an association of activists and NGOs providing aid at the border, and its members also routinely receive threatening comments on social media.

Cuts to humanitarian funding, including the suspension of funding from the U.S. Agency for International Development, which the Trump administration eliminated last year, have squeezed local groups. The drop in the number of crossings has also made it harder to sustain donor attention to the work that continues. Groups need to stay ready in case numbers rise again, and they are trying to support migrants already in Poland through asylum proceedings that run for years. “Donors will fund a crisis, but the work that comes afterwards is less attractive,” said Ania Romaniuk, integration advisor at EGALA Association, an NGO based in Białystok in north-eastern Poland, which provides Polish-language lessons for refugees and helps them find work, housing, schools, and medical care.

title: Dangerous Warning Signs from the First-Ever ATRC Case - Just Security
authors: Eric Lee, Brian Dooley, Suchita Uppal, Michael Mattler, Carol Rosenberg, Michael P. Scharf, Wells Dixon
description:

Ms. Haji Zada was unquestionably a part of “the people” to whom the Bill of Rights applies.
In accepting her removal, Ms. Haji Zada waived her right to appeal the removal order to the D.C.
What We Know About In re Haji Zada Because of the black-box nature of ATRC proceedings, the facts of In re Haji Zada remain obscure.
Despite this claim, the government never brought criminal charges against Ms. Haji Zada for material support for terrorism or conspiracy.
text:
On Sept. 11, the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (“ATRC”) unsealed records showing that the first-ever case brought in the tribunal’s 30-year history resulted in a successful deportation three weeks earlier. The Respondent, a Lawful Permanent Resident named Nazira Haji Zada, decided to accept deportation rather than mount a removal defense in a tribunal where respondents cannot review secret evidence nor challenge whether that evidence was obtained illegally. To do so, she conceded she is an “alien terrorist” and waived her right to appeal. As a result, the government achieved its objective without being required to defend the ATRC’s constitutionality, and Ms. Haji Zada was removed to Afghanistan on Aug. 25.

The outcome of In re Haji Zada undermines the argument advanced by some ATRC-watchers that the Trump administration’s invocation of the ATRC could be “good for the U.S. immigration system” and that “the ATRC may be less concerning than we think.” This argument, though based on reasonable concerns over the failures of the existing immigration court system, does not give sufficient weight to several critical dimensions of the ATRC process that were on display in In re Haji Zada.

Why the ATRC is Not Good for Non-Citizens and Democratic Rights

As an initial matter, the fact that Ms. Haji Zada decided to accept removal without invoking the extremely limited protections afforded to ATRC respondents is cause for concern. Without knowing the respondent’s motives for accepting removal, her decision indicates that the immense authority given to the executive branch through the ATRC can itself operate as a coercive element in the process, pressuring respondents to waive those protections and rendering them meaningless in practice.

The outcome also underscores the weight of the rights which the government was able to strip through the ATRC. By invoking the tribunal for the first time against a lawful permanent resident who had lived in the United States for years, the administration decided to test the ATRC and the lawfulness of its procedures under conditions where the constitutional status of the respondent was at its peak. Ms. Haji Zada was unquestionably a part of “the people” to whom the Bill of Rights applies. Nevertheless, when confronted with the ATRC process, she chose to give up her home and her lawful resident status to return to Afghanistan.

In other words, the administration not only succeeded in stripping her of her green card, it also stripped her of all of the protections of the Constitution which she had previously enjoyed during her residency through a process that more closely resembles a military tribunal, where defendants lack rights that are guaranteed in civil courts and can be convicted without the right to confront some of the evidence against them. The process also moved on a very rapid timeline: roughly six weeks passed between the Justice Department’s July 15 filing of the removal application and Ms. Haji Zada’s Aug. 25 deportation.

In re Haji Zada is also significant for what the Respondent was not able to do. In accepting her removal, Ms. Haji Zada waived her right to appeal the removal order to the D.C. Circuit, by which she may have tested the constitutionality of the ATRC procedures. These procedures bar respondents from suppressing evidence they allege was unlawfully obtained, and can deny them notice of whether it was gathered through coercion or in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

End-Running Article III Habeas Review

Those ATRC-watchers who believe that some good may come out of the ATRC point out, correctly, that the immigration court system is so stacked against non-citizens that there is little hope for fair adjudication through the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review. At the minimum, so the argument goes, a non-citizen placed into ATRC proceedings will appear before an Article III judge, rather than before immigration judges subject to White House political pressure.

This is a legitimate point, but it obscures how the ATRC also keeps (or, at least, appears to keep) detention challenges out of district court. It expressly bars habeas review of continued detention after a removal order, allowing only constitutional claims and only in the D.C. Circuit, and it routes challenges to detention pending appeal to the D.C. Circuit as well. Whether a respondent held before the hearing could petition a district court for habeas is untested. The ATRC also does not authorize release hearings for respondents who are not lawful permanent residents, and the same evidentiary rules (secret evidence, no confrontation) apply in ATRC release hearings for green card holders. And while it is also true that the administration is stretching the limits of statutory authority for mandatory detention of non-citizens, in hundreds or thousands of cases, non-citizens have won release from detention through writs of habeas corpus, with some federal judges issuing blistering decisions denouncing the administration’s unconstitutional detention practices.

Consider the case of Yaakub Vijandre,* a 39-year-old DACA recipient who was detained and put into removal proceedings last October based on the allegation that his social media posts and photojournalism constitute support for terrorism. In that case, his habeas petitions argue that the evidence the government presented to support its allegation of terrorism consisted entirely of political and religious speech that is protected by the First Amendment, and on that basis Mr. Vijandre was able to challenge the evidence in a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. On Sept. 28, a federal judge adopted a magistrate’s report and recommendation denying the Trump administration’s motion to dismiss his petition on jurisdictional grounds, setting the stage for the court to subject the government’s evidence to constitutional scrutiny. Had Mr. Vijandre been put into ATRC proceedings, he would have had no statutory ability to see the evidence against him, and no way to mount the defense that he is now making in federal district court, unless the government volunteered to provide him with more information than the statute required.

What We Know About In re Haji Zada

Because of the black-box nature of ATRC proceedings, the facts of In re Haji Zada remain obscure. The administration has given the most prominent public account of the evidence against Ms. Haji Zada in the press release the Justice Department published on September 11, the day the ATRC unsealed records showing Ms. Haji Zada had been deported.

In its press statement, the Justice Department pointed to little activity by the respondent herself, instead pointing to a terrorist plot that was planned by her relatives. The press release references Ms. Haji Zada’s decision to “sign a contract to sell the family house” and states that the family bought one-way tickets to Kabul, including for her, shortly before Election Day 2024. It implies the house sale was related to financing the plot, but offers little beyond general assertions that she “supported” it. Despite this claim, the government never brought criminal charges against Ms. Haji Zada for material support for terrorism or conspiracy. These facts come concerningly close to guilt-by-association based on family ties.

The government also claims it provided Ms. Haji Zada with “approximately half a terabyte of documents” about the case, but the government also stated in paragraph 11 of its July 15 filing to the ATRC that these documents were unclassified, and that the classified evidence was “the only evidence” that supported the case for deportation.

What the administration’s public statements do show, however, is a desire to press the advantage provided by its successful first use of the ATRC. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg stated in the July 30 press release that the administration “will use all the tools at our disposal, including this court, to remove foreign nationals who betray our values and exploit our goodwill by supporting ISIS and terrorist plots.” (Emphasis added). DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “Those who plot acts of terrorism against the United States have no place in our country. We will find them, and we will use every lawful tool available to remove them.”

An Extraordinary Court in Extraordinary Times

In re: Haji Zada involved accusations of association with or support for ISIS, but the administration has defined “terrorism” to include far more than criminal acts of political violence against civilians. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller called Alex Pretti a “domestic terrorist” after the U.S. citizen and VA nurse was fatally shot by federal immigration officials in Minneapolis in January, then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche referred to anti-ICE protesters in Chicago as “domestic terrorists,” and the administration has formally labeled “Antifa” (short for “anti-fascism”) as a domestic terrorist organization. As events dating back to January 6, 2021, demonstrate, those who hope the Trump administration will use the ATRC responsibly are expecting restraint from an administration that has almost never exercised it.

This context drives at the real problem with the ATRC. The danger posed by the ATRC is not the risk of misuse, the lack of sharply defined internal protocols or the untested nature of the statutory framework, it is the very nature of the ATRC itself. At its root, this is a domestic tribunal wherein the executive branch may deprive someone with constitutional rights of their liberty, relying on secret evidence. In the words of Justice Jackson,

“Security is like liberty, in that many are the crimes committed in its name… In the name of security, the police state justifies its arbitrary oppressions on evidence that is secret, because security might be prejudiced if it were brought to light in hearings. The plea that evidence of guilt must be secret is abhorrent to free men, because it provides a cloak for the malevolent, the misinformed, the meddlesome, and the corrupt to play the role of informer undetected and uncorrected.”

A bipartisan Congress granted the ATRC authority to the executive branch thirty years ago, and now the country—and the Constitution—are suffering the consequences.

name: Human Rights
title: Reader's letter: I want the same human rights for a stranger as I want for my own children
description:
Suddenly, people who had come to this country seeking refuge had become the focus of demonstrations outside the place where they were living.
I wanted those inside the hotel to know that not everyone in Southampton wanted them to feel unwelcome.
That was when I first came across Southampton Stand Up To Racism.
I had seen them become the focus of anger simply because they were seeking refuge here.
I want the same human rights for a stranger as I want for my own children.
text:
By Southampton resident (details supplied).

I first became aware that there were weekly protests outside an asylum seekers’ hotel in Portswood when I saw people gathering outside Highfield House Hotel, protesting against people seeking refuge here. Other people were turning up to counter-protest.

I have lived in the area for more than 20 years, but until the protests began I had not even realised that the hotel had been converted in 2020 to accommodate people seeking asylum. There had been very little discussion about it locally. Suddenly, people who had come to this country seeking refuge had become the focus of demonstrations outside the place where they were living.

I kept thinking about what that must feel like.

Imagine travelling a long way from home, perhaps because you are escaping danger, persecution or circumstances you can no longer live with, and finally arriving somewhere you hope will be safe — only to find people outside your accommodation shouting abuse and accusing you of things they know nothing about.

And I kept asking myself: What if I had been born somewhere else? What if my circumstances had been different? What if I had been the one who needed to flee?

One Friday after work, I found myself feeling uncomfortable sitting at home while, just around the corner, people who were already far from their families and everything they knew were facing a group of people shouting abuse and waving flags outside their accommodation.

I could have stayed at home. But it didn’t feel right.

I wanted those inside the hotel to know that not everyone in Southampton wanted them to feel unwelcome. So I went along to the counter-protest.

That was when I first came across Southampton Stand Up To Racism.

I remember hearing people say, “They’re illegal immigrants.”

I had never had a particularly strong view on immigration, but I started looking into what I was actually hearing. I learned that people have the right to seek asylum and that arriving by boat does not, by itself, make someone an “illegal immigrant”. Their asylum claims have to be assessed.

Then I heard other things: “They’re rapists.” “They’re fighting-age men.” “They’re dangerous.” I found myself asking: how can we know that about people we have never met?

Of course, if an individual commits a crime, they should be held accountable for their actions. That should apply to everyone. But that is very different from treating an entire group of people as though they are dangerous because of where they come from or because they are seeking asylum.

The more I listened, the more uncomfortable I became with the way a group of people I had never met were being spoken about as though they were all the same.

The “Patriots” say they are not racist. But standing there and listening to what was being shouted, I found it difficult to separate the arguments from the prejudice behind them. When I stripped away the different claims and slogans, what I heard was increasingly about people being targeted because they were different, foreign and vulnerable.

For me, that is what racism can look and sound like: prejudice dressed up as arguments, and fear turned into hostility towards people who have little power to defend themselves.

That was the point at which this stopped being an abstract argument about immigration for me. These were real people, living just around the corner. I had seen them become the focus of anger simply because they were seeking refuge here.

That is why I joined Southampton Stand Up To Racism.

And it is why I will be at the Bargate on Saturday 3 October.

I will be there because I know what it felt like the first time I stood outside that hotel. I remember looking across the road and thinking that, whatever else people might disagree about, those inside deserved to know that not everyone in Southampton wanted them to feel unwelcome.

On 3 October, I want to stand with people from across our city and send that same message again.

I’m not going because I want confrontation. I’m going because I don’t want silence to be mistaken for consent.

I want the people being targeted to know that they are not alone, and I want to show that the Southampton I know is a city where people can stand together despite their differences.

I want the same human rights for a stranger as I want for my own children.

That is why I stand up:

Peace over violence.

Solidarity over division.

Empathy over hate.

Community over fear.

If not me, then who? If not now, then when?

text:
NEW ORLEANS — Julian Curo-Churata, a 47-year-old illegal alien from Peru, passed away in ICE custody Sept. 29, 2026, at Ochsner LSU Health Monroe Medical Center in Monroe, Louisiana. The preliminary cause of death is unknown. An autopsy will determine the official cause of death. On Sept. 28, Curo was found to be in medical distress. At approximately 8:14 p.m. CDT, facility staff transported Curo-Churata to Ochsner LSU Health Monroe Medical Center for advanced medical treatment. Despite life-saving efforts, an on-duty physician pronounced Curo deceased at 4:01 a.m. CDT.

His background includes convictions for driving with expired vehicle registration, and a separate court judgment against him in favor of the Comptroller of Maryland. Curo entered the United States at an unknown date and location without inspection. Enforcement and Removal Operations Baltimore arrested Curo during a targeted enforcement operation June 27, 2026, and served him with a Notice to Appear. ERO Baltimore transferred him to ERO New Orleans custody June 29, 2026, and detained him at Richwood Correctional Center. On Sept. 18, 2026, an immigration judge denied Curo’s applications for relief and voluntary departure. He reserved his right to appeal.

While in custody, Curo received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.

Consistent with ICE policy, ERO New Orleans notified the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility through the Joint Intake Center. ERO New Orleans also notified Curo-Churata’s spouse, his attorney, and the Consulate General of Peru.

ICE makes official notifications to Congress, non-governmental organization stakeholders and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.

ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility, access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained noncitizen denied emergency care.

title: Trump's White House Press Ban Is Not Even Close to Legal | Balls and Strikes
description:
Last week, the Trump administration attempted to block journalists from Politico, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House, citing “national security” concerns.
No one actually believes these outlets endangered national security with their reporting; instead, the White House tried to ban outlets it dislikes.
And second, by deciding to revoke credentials based on the perspectives taken by the media organizations, the White House violated the First Amendment’s ban on viewpoint discrimination.
Even if the White House had satisfied constitutional due process requirements, though, the media organizations had strong First Amendment arguments in their favor.
In this case, Trump’s complaints about “fake news” make it pretty obvious that the White House sought to ban specific news outlets because of the viewpoint of their coverage.
text:
Last week, the Trump administration attempted to block journalists from Politico, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House, citing “national security” concerns. It did not succeed: Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee to the federal district court in Washington, D.C., issued a temporary restraining order that restored those outlets’ access after about 12 hours.

But that victory in court represents only a piece of the larger story about the Trump administration’s vendetta against the press. No matter how many judges rule in favor of the media organizations, the administration has proven it won’t stop attacking those who try to bring its lawlessness, corruption, and bullying to light. Its purpose in doing so is to create an environment in which journalists feel besieged and thus less likely to investigate the government. And the administration has largely succeeded in creating that environment, even with its many losses in court.

The litigation between the White House and the media organizations shows how frequently the administration uses “national security” as a magic phrase to justify its actions. No one actually believes these outlets endangered national security with their reporting; instead, the White House tried to ban outlets it dislikes. Trump said as much when he announced the ban, posting on Truth Social that these outlets “constantly write or report fiction or lies.” Most administrations dislike the scrutiny of the news media, but never before has a president taken such drastic steps to clamp down on reporting.

The affected outlets quickly filed a lawsuit in federal court, alleging that the administration had violated their constitutional rights in two ways. First, they said, by arbitrarily revoking the passes without notice or any opportunity to be heard, the White House had infringed on their due process rights as protected by the Fifth Amendment. And second, by deciding to revoke credentials based on the perspectives taken by the media organizations, the White House violated the First Amendment’s ban on viewpoint discrimination.

The media organizations had a very forceful case. Multiple decisions from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit dating back almost fifty years have established the process a president must follow to constitutionally revoke a “hard pass,” and revoking badge access without warning does not suffice. In his opinion granting the requested restraining order, Kelly held that the Trump administration had not complied with due process requirements. He did not rule on the First Amendment claims, in large part because the administration’s procedural sloppiness made it an easy case.

Even if the White House had satisfied constitutional due process requirements, though, the media organizations had strong First Amendment arguments in their favor. Some government spaces, like public parks or sidewalks, constitute public forums in which the government cannot make decisions based on content—for example, allowing rallies for charities but not for political parties. In nonpublic forums like the White House briefing room, the government can make content-based decisions about access—for example, allowing news media organizations but preventing access by the general public. But it cannot make viewpoint-based decisions. In other words, viewpoint discrimination is never permissible, even in nonpublic forums where the government has more power to constitutionally limit access.

In this case, Trump’s complaints about “fake news” make it pretty obvious that the White House sought to ban specific news outlets because of the viewpoint of their coverage. It is almost always impossible under the First Amendment to ban some speakers but not others just because the government doesn’t like what some speakers are saying.

Because viewpoint discrimination is treated as the most offensive type of government regulation of speech, the White House had to invoke “national security” to try to explain its actions. But even though national security often functions as a free pass for administrations asking judges for permission to do things that would never fly in another setting, it made little sense in this instance. Kelly said as much in granting the temporary restraining order, dryly observing that “nothing in the record…suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” and noting Trump’s myopic focus on “the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.” Donald Trump opening his mouth to tell the truth made it impossible for his lawyers to depict the government’s actions as something lawful.

Though the press prevailed in this case, Trump and his administration’s actions have real consequences. Litigation may slow or even stop some of what the administration is trying to do, but lawsuits can’t repair the weakened political and social environment created by a president and executive branch committed to constantly undermining First Amendment values. And when the press becomes the story, it makes it harder for the public to see coverage of the government’s failures. A public distracted by a press freedom dispute, rather than reading about the administration’s latest corrupt actions, is exactly what Trump wants.

text:
Last week, the Trump administration moved to cancel millions of dollars in funding for programs for illegal aliens and foreign nationals as part of an $810 million pocket rescission. The rescission cancellation is the administration’s latest effort to combat illegal immigration and put American citizens first.

According to a White House memo published Friday, cutting these programs will provide savings to Americans, help further eliminate wasteful spending, and rather than welcoming illegal aliens, ensure they are being held accountable. Of the $810 million recission, funding designated specifically for anti-borders programs and grants included:

$567 million from Health and Human Services (HHS) for nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) with programs facilitating illegal immigration and exploiting unaccompanied children

$70 million for institutions importing foreign students and faculty to the United States

$50 million from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Education (DOE) providing legal aid for illegal aliens and teaching encouraging foreign nationals to take advantage of our education system and avoid law enforcement

The administration’s move takes strides towards easing the financial burden of illegal immigration on American taxpayers, which FAIR estimates to be at least $150.7 billion annually. While some appropriators in Congress have pushed back, and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) is set to issue a report against the practice, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russ Vought indicated the administration is moving ahead. He described the rescission as “an attempt to get at the border industrial complex, which furthered illegal immigration. It is another aspect of shutting off the number of people that can come into the system… and then getting at the funding source.”

FAIR looks forward to continued work with Congress and the White House to ensure illegal immigration is never rewarded, nor foreign nationals baselessly offered services at the expense of American taxpayers.

description:

People placed into expedited removal are often deported within a single day, making it virtually impossible to consult with an attorney or gather evidence.
Mandatory detention: Depriving people of liberty without due process IIRIRA didn’t just make deporting people easier.
IIRIRA vastly expanded mandatory detention by requiring the detention of noncitizens who are “applicants for admission” into the country.
In January 2025, President Trump signed the Laken Riley Act, a bipartisan law that broadened the criteria for mandatory detention.
text:
Thirty years ago, President Bill CIinton signed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) into law, creating legal tools that have allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to quickly implement its agenda of mass detention and deportation. Together, these laws immediately increased the number of people who were subject to deportation and detention and vastly expanded the overlap between the criminal and immigration systems. Over time, IIRIRA and AEDPA built the foundation for the immigration system the United States has today—one that strips immigrants of due process, criminalizes them, and continues to expand detention.

Supercharged by two rounds of federal reconciliation funding in which Congress bypassed the annual appropriations process to award a total of $240 billion for immigration enforcement, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have more money than ever, magnifying the harms of the 1996 laws to devastating effect. Worse yet, lawmakers continue their attempts to double down on IIRIRA’s approach by introducing a slate of bills that would further gut due process and impose severe consequences in people’s immigration cases. If we are to build an immigration system that prioritizes human dignity and due process over humiliation and punishment, we must first understand the policies that laid the groundwork for the Trump administration’s agenda today.

Expedited removal: How the Trump administration is bypassing immigration due process

In its efforts to deport as many people as quickly as possible, the Trump administration has relied heavily on expedited removal, a fast-tracked deportation mechanism created by IIRIRA that bypasses typical immigration proceedings. People placed in this category do not get a hearing with a judge. Instead, immigration officers decide if a person’s detention and deportation are lawful. Past administrations primarily applied expedited removal for people who were encountered by immigration enforcement within 100 miles of a U.S. land border and who had been in the country for less than two weeks. But the first and second Trump administrations expanded the use of expedited removal nationwide and increased the time threshold to two years.

People placed into expedited removal are often deported within a single day, making it virtually impossible to consult with an attorney or gather evidence. Trump’s expansion of expedited removal has been challenged by advocates in court who have raised due process concerns, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit recently sided with the administration, citing IIRIRA more than 20 times in its decision.

Mandatory detention: Depriving people of liberty without due process

IIRIRA didn’t just make deporting people easier. It also made the act of detaining people without bond hearings—called mandatory detention—commonplace. A bond hearing gives people the chance to be released while their immigration case proceeds, which in turn enables them to prepare for hearings, meet with a lawyer, and remain in their community while they wait for their time in court. IIRIRA vastly expanded mandatory detention by requiring the detention of noncitizens who are “applicants for admission” into the country. This practice has largely meant that asylum seekers presenting themselves to immigration officers at the border or ports of entry have been placed in mandatory detention with no opportunity to see a judge to request release on bond.

In July 2025, the Department of Homeland Security issued a memo stating that it would now consider anyone who entered the country without inspection as an “applicant for admission,” effectively ending bond hearings for many undocumented people, regardless of how long they have been living in the country. In response, attorneys filed tens of thousands of habeas corpus petitions in federal court to challenge their clients’ detention. This year, by early August, more than 11,800 people had been released from detention as a result of a federal court order, nearly 10 times the number during the same period in 2025. Nine federal appeals courts have rejected the administration’s mandatory detention policy, resulting in a circuit court split on the issue that could prompt U.S. Supreme Court review. In the meantime, some undocumented immigrants are being granted bond hearings while others are not, depending on which circuit court has jurisdiction over their cases.

The Trump administration did not need the Supreme Court, however, to expand mandatory detention. In January 2025, President Trump signed the Laken Riley Act, a bipartisan law that broadened the criteria for mandatory detention. For the first time, the law empowers ICE to detain people without bond hearings based on arrests, charges, or even allegations involving certain theft-related crimes, without requiring a conviction. The Laken Riley Act builds on the framework established by IIRIRA and AEDPA, further tying immigration detention to the criminal justice system.

The myth of immigrant criminality and its harms

Falsely connecting immigrants with crime has roots in the country’s early racial exclusion laws, and this harmful narrative continues to drive policies that entangle the immigration system with the criminal justice system. Congress created the “aggravated felony” category for immigration law purposes through the Anti–Drug Abuse Act of 1988 to cover three offenses: murder, drug trafficking, and firearm trafficking. Congress has since added other offenses to the list, but the most substantial changes were implemented through AEDPA and IIRIRA in 1996. These laws widened the category considerably to add nonviolent offenses—and even some crimes classified by states as misdemeanors. The term is thus misleading: an offense need not be aggravated or classified as a felony under state law to trigger serious immigration consequences.

People deemed to have committed an aggravated felony under these immigration laws are not only subject to mandatory detention but also, in some cases, expedited removal and a lifetime ban on legally returning to the United States if deported. These severe immigration consequences further compound the disproportionately harmful outcomes for Black and Latino immigrants that already exist in the criminal justice system due to racial bias. Compared to non-Black immigrants, for example, Black immigrants are detained for longer periods, are more likely to be placed in solitary confinement, and are subject to higher rates of violence and abuse in detention.

text:
On 3 September 2026 the Home Office published its Autumn Immigration Rules update. Key changes include new protections for Skilled Worker visa holders who are victims of modern slavery, measures to prevent abuse of fee waiver and biometrics processes, and updates to support the UK rejoining Erasmus+ from January 2027. There are also some useful expansions of permitted visitor route activities for those receiving training or coming to the UK for creative purposes.

Further details of the changes are outlined below, including when they come into effect.

Changes to Appendix Skilled Worker to support victims of modern slavery

Skilled Worker visa holders are not normally permitted to take up other work if they are not continuing to work in the job they are sponsored to do. However, from 8 October 2026 this restriction may be lifted for any Skilled Worker who has been recognised as a victim of modern slavery.

The liberalisation of work conditions will be restricted to those who have received a positive Conclusive Grounds decision via the National Referral Mechanism.

Details of how the process will work in practice are yet to be released by the Home Office, but once notified of the change to their immigration conditions, an individual will be allowed to work with minimal restrictions (including undertaking self-employment and voluntary work) for the rest of their existing Skilled Worker visa. The remaining restriction is that they will not be allowed to work as a professional sportsperson or sports coach. There will be no change to the immigration restriction prohibiting a Skilled Worker from accessing prescribed public funds.

This change, combined with the recently published temporary arrangement confirming the Home Office won't curtail the immigration permission of adult social care workers following sponsor licence revocation, could mean that victims have greater incentive to come forward and report modern slavery.

The Government is also taking other measures to combat worker exploitation. Earlier this month, the Government named nearly 660 employers who failed to pay staff the National Minimum Wage, returning £4 million directly to workers.

The Home Office is also continuing to consider the sponsorship system reforms indicated in last year's immigration white paper. Any reforms in this area will aim to put more responsibility and accountability on effective and responsible sponsors. Potentially the revised system may reduce the risk of worker exploitation by making it easier for work route visa holders to move between licensed sponsors throughout the duration of their visa.

Change to when a fee waiver extends immigration permission

A change is made to para 34G(4) of the Immigration Rules. This confirms that when a fee waiver application has been made, the date of the subsequent immigration application will only be the date of the fee waiver request if the immigration application is the human rights application connected to the fee waiver request.

The change is in place for immigration applications made on or after 8 October 2026.

The amendment is aimed at preventing the exploitation of the fee waiver process by applicants who use the fee waiver process to access a statutory extension of their immigration permission ahead of submitting a non-human rights application.

One consequence of this change is that some potential work route applicants may need to make an application for entry clearance rather than seeking to extend their permission in-country as an overstayer. The options in each case should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Varying immigration applications – single period to enrol biometrics

Where an application is made on or after 8 October 2026 to vary an outstanding application, the biometrics must still be enrolled by the deadline applicable to the previous application. In essence, there will only be a single period to enrol biometrics.

Again, this change is targeted at preventing abuse by applicants who aim to prolong a statutory extension of their permission by making an application and then varying it multiple times without enrolling their biometrics. This has been effective in the past because an application can't be substantively considered until the validity requirements for it (including biometric enrolment) have been met.

Changes relating to the UK rejoining the Erasmus+ programme

The UK has agreed with the EU to rejoin the Erasmus+ programme for education, training, youth and sport from 1 January 2027.

For applications made on or after 8 October 2026, the following changes are made to facilitate immigration processes relating to this development:

Appendix Government Authorised Exchange schemes is updated to add the 'Erasmus+' scheme on the same basis as other scheme requirements and conditions;

Appendix V is updated to permit visitors participating in an Erasmus+ project to study at UK state funded schools and academies for up to 6 months, subject to child safeguarding and other eligibility requirements being met;

Appendix Student is amended to enable students undertaking a course as part of the Erasmus+ programme to be sponsored regardless of whether the course of study leads to an approved qualification;

A new category of permitted activities for visitors entitled 'Erasmus+ activities' has been added, enabling Erasmus+ participants to carry out specific programme-related training, education and work experience activities.

The permitted activities for visitors are expanded as mentioned in the section below.

Changes to permitted activities for visitors

The changes below apply to those who make an application for a visitor visa or for entry as a visitor on or after 8 October 2026.

Participation in workshops, debates and Skills Competitions

Partly to further facilitate participation in Erasmus+, all visitors (including those not participating in Erasmus+) will be allowed to participate in workshops and debates, and to attend Skills Competitions.

Receiving training in the UK

When visitors come to the UK to undertake training, they will no longer have to show that this training is unavailable in their home country.

Attending rehearsals for visiting artists, entertainers and musicians

Visitors who are artists, entertainers, and musicians will be permitted to attend rehearsals in addition to performances.

Permitted activities for entertainment staff

A new definition of 'entertainment staff' is introduced for visitor route purposes, meaning an individual employed by an organisation, entertainer, musician, or artist to support in the preparation, setting up and running of an event held within the UK.

Entertainment staff may support a visiting artist, entertainer or musician provided they are employed by that person outside the UK and are assisting them in connection with the same permitted creative activities their employer is coming to the UK to participate in.

Changes to refusal grounds – frustrating immigration controls

With effect from 8 October 2026, a change to Part Suitability confirms that if an applicant has previously acted to frustrate immigration controls (e.g. by failing to report for bail or absconding from bail or custody), they will be classed as having been in breach of immigration laws when making an in-country application for permission to stay.

The amendment aligns in-country refusal grounds with those for entry clearance.

title: ICE is detaining pregnant immigrants. Most Americans say they shouldn't. - The 19th News
description:
More than half of Black and Hispanic Americans say they should never be held in immigration detention.
Even among Republicans, only 30 percent said they support a general policy of detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants.
The 19th has been reporting on Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) detentions of pregnant, nursing and postpartum immigrants since President Donald Trump’s second inauguration.
Americans broadly support access to pregnancy-related healthcare for detained immigrants.
If pregnant, postpartum or nursing immigrants are detained, the poll found, Americans broadly believe those people should be given basic pregnancy-related healthcare.
text:
More than two-thirds of Americans say that immigrants who are pregnant, nursing or have recently given birth should generally not be held in immigration detention, according to a new 19th News/YouGov poll.

The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has led to more arrests, detentions and deportations of pregnant and postpartum immigrants, who are more medically vulnerable than the general population. About 29 percent of respondents said that immigrants who are pregnant, have recently given birth or are nursing should be detained only in “exceptional circumstances,” and 41 percent said they should not be kept in detention facilities at all.

Women are more likely to oppose the policy.

Only 12 percent of women believe that immigrants facing deportation should be held in detention even if they are pregnant, postpartum or nursing a baby, compared with 72 percent who say this group never should be or should be only in exceptional circumstances.

Men are overall more likely to support the detention of pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants, but still, most men — 68 percent — say they should not be held or be held only in exceptional circumstances.

Overall, Americans don’t agree with the administration’s approach.

There’s no demographic subset of Americans polled that says immigrants facing deportation should, as a rule, be held in detention even if they are pregnant, postpartum or nursing a baby. More than half of Black and Hispanic Americans say they should never be held in immigration detention.

Even among Republicans, only 30 percent said they support a general policy of detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants. Meanwhile, 55 percent either said these people should not be detained or should be detained only in exceptional circumstances.

The poll also showed that most Democrats and Independents — 85 percent and 57 percent, respectively — believe the Trump administration is doing “too much” when it comes to deporting immigrants. A majority of women, 55 percent, also said they believe the administration is doing “too much,” compared with 45 percent of men surveyed.

Here’s why we asked.

The 19th has been reporting on Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) detentions of pregnant, nursing and postpartum immigrants since President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. In March, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed that 363 pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants were deported between January 1, 2025, and February 16, 2026, out of 498 who were detained and then left an ICE facility during that time, either via deportation or release.

A Biden-era policy directed ICE not to detain, arrest or take into custody pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding people simply for breaking immigration laws, except under “exceptional circumstances.” The Trump administration has not formally reversed that policy, but reports from across the country confirm that ICE has detained numerous pregnant immigrants since Trump took office.

The Department of Homeland Security has said it detains these immigrants infrequently and that those who are detained receive “comprehensive medical care.”

Over the last 18 months, The 19th has spoken with several women who say that they were detained despite having no criminal record or having only traffic violations. Several had pending asylum applications.

Many of them shared that they did not receive basic healthcare — including breast pumps, prenatal visits, vitamins or extra food — while detained. Nayra Guzmán, said she did not have a bed to sleep on, despite being in recovery for a recent Cesarean section. Amanda Isabel Fanego Cardoso said she was diagnosed with preeclampsia and gestational diabetes after being released but was not made aware of those conditions while in detention.

Americans broadly support access to pregnancy-related healthcare for detained immigrants.

If pregnant, postpartum or nursing immigrants are detained, the poll found, Americans broadly believe those people should be given basic pregnancy-related healthcare. About two-thirds of respondents — 67 percent — said these immigrants should be given breast pumps, and about 77 percent said they should receive prenatal care.

About 78 percent said that if immigration authorities separate a parent from an infant, they should be required to give the parent some contact with their baby.

How does this tie into the November elections?

Control of both the U.S. House and Senate are up for grabs in the November midterm elections, and it’s not clear yet how voters’ views on immigration policy and the Trump administration will affect their decisions.

Immigration is not currently a top issue for voters, but combined with Trump’s broader disapproval and weakened support for the GOP among Latinos — the group most affected by the administration’s immigration crackdown — the issue could still play an influential role in Florida, Texas, Arizona and beyond.

If Democrats win majorities in Congress, their party could exert greater oversight of the agencies carrying out Trump’s immigration agenda.

For example, Congress could revive a Biden-era rule that required DHS to report twice a year on how many pregnant, nursing or postpartum immigrants were held in immigration detention and include a “detailed justification” for every detained immigrant in these categories.

The 19th/YouGov poll was conducted online from September 18 to 24 among 2,357 adults, including an oversampling of 18- to 29-year-olds. The margin of error for the overall sample is ± 2.5 points.
